utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This morning we begin the hearing of witnesses in the Defence case. Mr. Kay, in your new role as the court-assigned counsel, you will lead the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: My Lord, thank you. The first issue I want to deal with is the first witness, concerning Professor Avramov. Professor Avramov is here and present at court today and indeed was good enough to give me the opportunity to speak to her for several hours last night and to discuss the terms of her involvement in this case and evidence that she could give in the interests of the accused. I know, although I've had no direct communication from the accused himself - I went to the Detention Unit yesterday to see if he would see me at a pre-arranged time, but that was not so, and this morning he did not want to see me either - but I happen to know from other sources that he would like me to make an application in relation to the modalities concerning, as far as I know, certainly this witness, but modality 2 which deals with the examination of witnesses: "The accused may, with the leave of the Trial Chamber, continue to participate actively in the conduct of his case including, where appropriate, examining witnesses following examination by court-assigned counsel." And from the information that I have received indirectly from the accused, he would like me to apply to the Court that he could take certainly this witness first, and probably - I don't know whether this is the case because I haven't been spoken to directly by him - all witnesses, but certainly I can make the application for this witness. So that's my first application this morning in relation to this witness before she's called into court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, let me just understand what you have said. You have tried to communicate with the accused, and you said you were not successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Be plain as to why you were not successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He declined to see us, and there is a channel through which we can obviously communicate, through the Registry of the court, that enables appointments to be made. So I went to the Detention Unit yesterday at a pre-arranged time in the hope that he would see us so that we could discuss issues, but that was not fruitful, and likewise this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In doing that, you're of course acting pursuant to the Chamber's order that you endeavour to obtain instructions from the accused. But I understand you to say that the accused refused to see you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. So I wasn't able to fulfil that aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me turn to the application that you have made on his behalf. You rightly adverted to paragraph 2 of the Chamber's order. The main rationale for the Chamber assigning you as counsel for the accused is that the accused, on medical grounds, medical advice, is not fit to represent himself, and it would contradict the logic of that order were the Chamber, at any rate in this first phase of the Defence case, to allow the accused to commence examination-in-chief. The Chamber's order does make it clear that, where appropriate, the accused will be allowed to ask questions following your examination-in-chief. We do not -- we do not rule it out, but certainly we would not consider allowing the accused to commence examination-in-chief of -- of these witnesses. We may consider, in an appropriate case, the accused asking questions following your examination-in-chief. That is a matter which the Chamber will take up on a case-by-case basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well. I've made my application. I can't take that matter any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Call your first witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Professor Avramov, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I wish to say that you took away my right to Defence and put it in the hands of Mr. Kay, who does not represent me. He represents you. With Mr. Kay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we will not rehearse ground that we have already covered. I don't like that. I will not allow it. If you have a new point to make, then make it, but I don't want to hear the same tired refrain. If you have a new point to make, make it and make it quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, Defence through an imposed lawyer is simple legal fiction. I insist that you give me back my right to Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm stopping you. You have already indicated that you will appeal the decision. That's -- you're perfectly entitled to do that. Mr. Kay, your first witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not hearing you any more on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In those circumstances, Your Honour, I'll call Professor Avramov.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Professor Avramov, thank you for coming to court this morning, and I know you speak English as well as, obviously, B/C/S, and we'll conduct this examination, you can give your evidence in either language, as you prefer.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I prefer to talk English -- I'm sorry, Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Serbian?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You'll forgive me for addressing you in English, but I appreciate the fact that you prefer to speak in your native language.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Professor Avramov, if you could tell the Court, first of all, about your background. You are a university professor in law; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. For 40 years I was a professor at the Faculty of Law in Belgrade. I'm retired now, but still from time to time I teach postgraduate courses and graduate courses, in Belgrade, of course. I don't know exactly what you're interested in from my curriculum vitae. I studied a long time ago, before the Second World War. I studied at the great universities of Europe. I had the honour of having exceptional professors as Hans Kelsen, Schutzenberger, who was my mentor when I did my master's degree in London, and I got my Ph.D. I also have a Doctor Iuris, but I got my Ph.D. at the Faculty of Law in Belgrade. I defended a dissertation from the field of legal philosophy. Rebus Sic Standibus. I worked as a professor, and during my career I became head of the department for international law and international relations at the Faculty of Law in Belgrade. I was there until my retirement. Also, for almost 20 years, I was director for the -- of the Institute for International Law, also at the Faculty of Law in Belgrade. I was very active in legal associations -- law associations in Belgrade and in international law associations. I was president of the Yugoslav Association for International Law, and in 1980, I was elected president of the International Law Association. In 1968, I was elected co-chairman of the International Conference for Peace and Disarmament, also with its seat in London, and I was also on the executive board of the World Association for Struggling Against Nuclear War and Nuclear Armament. I participated in many international conferences and gatherings. Let me mention The Hague here and also New York, Japan, Tokyo, New Delhi, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Mr. Kay, there is a point I want to raise with you. It is clear that the professor is well qualified but I observe she's not giving evidence as an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. She had a particular role in events which Your Honours will hear about as we move past her background and deal with her involvement. Perhaps if I can take that up now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Also, Professor, you were a legal advisor for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: For many years I was a member of the legal council of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, yes, that is correct, in my capacity as head of department for international law. It was customary for the head of the department to be a member of the legal council of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs, yes. I think I was there for perhaps over 15 years, perhaps even some 20 years or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And just again as background, in fact, one of your law students was -- was Mr. Milosevic. He studied under you some years ago.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Correct. Yes, Mr. Milosevic got his degree from the Faculty of Law. And as professor, I did have contact with him. He was an excellent student. He displayed a great degree of interest, especially in international economic law. He had a particular characteristic. He had intellectual curiosity, if I can say it in English. After my lectures, he always put questions. He always sought additional explanations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Once Mr. Milosevic had finished studying under you, how did you next come across him in your professional life? At what sort of period?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: It is very hard to do this, but I'll try to remember. Mr. Milosevic came to the university. He came to the library. He took books from the library even after he got his degree. We would meet each other, and our encounters were always on a friendly note, cordial, the proper kind of encounter between a professor and his or her former students. After that, I had no further contact with him up to the moment when Mr. Milosevic - this was the end of March, 1991 - he called me and invited me to take part in preliminary negotiations on a very high intellectual level with colleagues from Croatia in order to view the backdrop, actually, or perhaps to put it better, the consequences of the crisis that had already engulfed Yugoslavia to a considerable extent. If you're interested, perhaps that would be of significance, of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have you ever been a member of any of his political parties?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: No. For a brief period of time I was a member of the Communist Party, then I was excluded from the party, expelled, and after that I never joined any other political party. That was in the 1970s when I left the party, and after that I never joined any political party. When Mr. Milosevic called me, invited me, I said that to him. I said that I was not a member of any political party, and he said, "Does that matter?" Those were his words. I said, "You see, we need to clarify certain matters. I have no intention of going into political life, particularly because I never held political office ever in my life," and he repeated that to me. "I did not invite you in that capacity. I am interested in your expert knowledge, and I believe that at this critical point in time in our country your help could be useful." When we discussed the ways in which I could be useful, he said to me, "Isn't it clear to you that we are in a serious crisis, that the country is in a serious crisis?" And I said, "Yes, of course. You know that I published some very, very critical articles, and not only that, in 1987 I published a book entitled the Control Over Foreign Policy." I was highly irritated as a member of the legal council of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. There were representatives there of all the federal units, and I don't know how familiar you are with this or actually with our constitution, the constitution that was in force then, as a matter of fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Permit me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I stop you. May I ask that you just answer the questions put to you by counsel. And there is a question that I would like to ask you. You mentioned that you were expelled from the Communist Party.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why was that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, I was not disciplined. They were quite right when they expelled me. I voted against decisions that were being passed. Any party calls for party discipline and I am a very undisciplined person, perhaps a bit of an individualist, and that was the reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You had done some research before 1991 on the republics of Yugoslavia in which you had observed issues within those republics concerning their foreign policies; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. That's what I wanted to point out. Of course, as a member of the legal council, I received many documents because we discussed different aspects of foreign policy. I then came to the conclusion that every republic had a foreign policy of its own and that we're moving towards a disintegration. I drew the attention of the council to that itself, and then I wrote about it because I was highly irritated by it. So I wrote this book entitled Control Over Foreign Policy in which I underlined that we do not have any control over foreign policy, that we no longer have a single foreign policy, that foreign policy is being branched off into six federal units. That was the main point. And that was not the only thing I pointed out. I pointed out that some federal units had already abused certain things because the constitution made it possible for federal units to have something at local level. I mean, they could not conclude contracts, no, but compacts - that's the English word - they could conclude compacts. However, particularly in the case of Croatia, and Slovenia for that matter, there were major deviations, and that is what I dealt with in that particular book. It was criticised, the book was. They thought that I went too far. Our foreign policy at the time criticised it, too, but that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In March 1991, at that period, Yugoslavia was in crisis because the issue of the secession of Slovenia and Croatia was forefront of the politics of the time.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: The secession hadn't taken place at the time. The crisis demonstrated itself in the fact that Slovenia and Croatia simply refused to respect federal laws and didn't want to do that. That's where it started from. Other than that, certain illegal organisations -- I showed you a document. It was the title page of an illegal magazine. I have to say that Yugoslavia was in a crisis in a certain way ever since 1945 until 1990. In a certain way, Yugoslavia was often on the brink of civil war. The cause of that was the resistance or the protest that was there. There was a very specific situation that played itself out, as you know. In the territory of Yugoslavia we had a liberation war, and after the war there was the Independent State of Croatia that was formed during the war which was under the protectorate of the Nazi Germany, and a large number of Nazi-leaning Croats emigrated. From 1945 they immediately organised their illegal groups, and later these illegal groups were turned into terrorist organisations. I must say that from 1945 to 1980, this terrorist organisation of Croatia, which later in 1991 entered Croatia and had the main word there, there were 430 terrorist acts committed against Yugoslavia in that period. Perhaps somebody recalls the murder of our ambassadors; for example, Ambassador Rolovic in Stockholm. I don't know if you recall the hijacking of the Yugoslav aeroplane which was downed over Czechoslovakia and everyone was killed in that incident. There was a lot about the terrorist acts. Actually, they were not -- Lockerbie was very much talked about but the terrorist acts against Yugoslavia were not discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I can just ask you about the context of 1991 and the role that President Milosevic invited you to undertake pre- the secession of Slovenia. What was the purpose of your role?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: What I have just told you. I have told you in order for you to be able to look at a certain continuity that exists, because without this continuity, you cannot understand everything that was happening from 1991 onwards. But I want to come back to what you asked me. Mr. Milosevic told me the following: "We are in a very serious crisis. I have come to the idea that it would be very good that independent intellectuals from Croatia -- from Serbia, together with the independent intellectuals from Croatia, because the central question was the relationship between Serbia and Croatia, between Zagreb and Belgrade. This is something that has been a thread throughout the history of Yugoslavia. So these intellectuals should review possible - I emphasise possible - consequences of the destruction of Yugoslavia. I told him then, because I was doing some research before that period, between 1980 and 1985 but also earlier, at the Rome military archives, also military archives in Freiburg, in Germany, the state archives in Bonn, and also in the public record office in London. Also I did some research in Washington. I was working on this research for a book which I published which should not have been published. It was banned and then it was finally published in 1989. It's called Genocide in Yugoslavia in the Light of International Law. This book was translated into English. I hope that you have it. Because I was working in these archives, I said to Mr. Milosevic in our conversation at the time, I told him two things. I must admit that today I regret it. One of my views has been completely confirmed, but the other opinion that I had has not been confirmed. It was quite the opposite, actually. But I told him that I had been following from the beginning the illegal movement of the so-called Croatian liberation movement from 1945 onwards, and all the transformations of that movement, that they had gone very far, that they had very deep roots in the country. They had roots in the party itself, the Communist Party and the Communist Party leadership. This illegal movement had very deep roots in Germany and in the United States, but their situation was that they had infiltrated various services as an anti-communist movement. However, this was a deception, because that movement at the same time worked along two lines; along the line of Moscow and the line of Washington, and their thesis was to achieve independence regardless of the means, with or without the assistance of the communists. Yugoslavia must die. Yugoslavia must disappear, either with the help of the Bolsheviks or the capitalists, we don't care. That was their main idea. And I told Mr. Milosevic this, and I also told him that it seemed to me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I just ask you, your book Genocide In Yugoslavia, which I have not had the good fortune of reading, what period did it cover? The genocidal acts to which you must have referred in that book, related to what period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It refers to the period 1941 to 1945, but the monitoring of the illegal movement continued later than that. Only in 1989 I had the opportunity to actually publish in book, but I had finished it for publication much earlier, because genocide was a taboo and it was something that it was not possible to discuss. I will be happy to send you the English translation of that book. When I had the opportunity, when there was a considerable degree of liberalisation in the regime and when it was possible to publish this, I revised the book a little bit and added something so that I included the illegal movements in the period also up to the outbreak of the crisis. So that is the period that it covers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see this witness as --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, just for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see this witness largely as setting the legal and historical background to the events, and that is why I am allowing some latitude in the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour, and there are specifics as well which start from 1991 onwards, and the professor has been keen to put that information before the Court, and in many respects it adds skin and muscle to what the bones of her evidence is and how she became to be involved in the events that took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, that answer deviated completely from the question you asked. The question you asked was about communications between Mr. Milosevic and the professor, a very pertinent question in view of the start of the answer. Now, I would be very grateful if that issue were followed up, because it goes to the attitude of the accused at a particular relevant time in the events that we're considering.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a moment, Professor. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A very short point. Evidence of background has come from the Prosecution typically via expert witnesses. We were concerned that this witness might be giving expert evidence but received confirmation from the accused's associates that she was going to be purely factual. I'm entirely content, of course, to listen to the evidence without any further comment or interruption, but if matters of expertise are dealt with, I may not be able to deal with them comprehensively in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, bear that in mind. I did raise that earlier with you, that she's not giving evidence as an expert. Were she giving evidence as an expert, then a report would have had to be presented to the Prosecution and to the Chamber as a whole, and the Prosecution would have had the benefit of reading the report and preparing for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I appreciate that, but obviously how this witness arrived in 1991 to be contacted by President Milosevic is of relevance, and that's really how this background comes in. It carries with it other elements, but as far as her particular role was concerned and her standing, that that's how it comes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Direct her now to the specific question raised by Judge Bonomy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And endeavour to, as we say in the common law, to control the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm giving some latitude here for the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: -- these are quite specific facts which I would like to state, and they are of key importance and in the context of what I talked about with Mr. Milosevic. And this part of my testimony -- actually, this part of what I told him came true afterwards. The things that did not come true out of the things that I told Mr. Milosevic at the time was that Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond regardless of all the negative circumstances that we might encounter as a result of that -- the activities of the subversive terrorist movements that we were faced with for which the General Staff in March, already, said that we are faced with the same enemies that we faced in 1941, therefore, this is something that we have to pay attention to. What did I say that did not come true? I tried to convince Mr. Milosevic that the United Nations, under any conditions, will not recognise secession.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Professor, if you could just answer my questions on this issue as we will actually lead into those -- those areas through the questions, because it's very important, as you will appreciate, on the issue of individual criminal responsibility of Mr. Milosevic, that we also deal with matters involving him and the generality of the issues will come with that. In March 1991, when you were asked to take part in negotiations with other intellectuals from the republics, was -- what was the purpose of those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Just from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just from Croatia. Not from Slovenia in March 1991? Right.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: No. No. Only from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of those negotiations from President Milosevic's conversation with you?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I have just told you. Mr. Milosevic wanted to let the other side know, as well as the public, about the terrible consequences of the destruction of Yugoslavia, and that is why the composition from our side and from the Croats' side was such that it was to cover four important spheres from our political life. I was in charge of international law, there was an economist who covered economic relations and the economic consequences in case this happened, then political consequences and constitutional consequences. So that both from the Croat and the Serbian side we had experts from different fields. The reaction of Mr. Milosevic is extremely important. Because my reaction was quite dramatic - maybe I had overdone it but maybe not, I know that I was very irritated with all the things that were going on in Yugoslavia, and at one point I told Mr. Milosevic, "I'm afraid that it is all in vain. Don't you see how things are going, which direction the policies of the country's leadership are going to?" And to that he replied calmly, "I call on you to stay calm and to take part in this discussion, and then when these gentlemen -" or comrades, as he called them - "find out how serious the consequences would be, they will come to themselves and they will stop with all this fanaticism and this independence. They will come to their senses." As I said, in a way he was obsessed with this idea that Yugoslavia had to be preserved, and that was the topic of our conversation and his appeal for maximum tolerance. And I must tell you that maximum tolerance, this is -- we approached these negotiations in a very friendly and very ethical way. I have to say one thing: Mr. Mesic testified before this Tribunal, and he mentioned me twice. What he said were pure lies. I listened to that on television. He implied that we, at those meetings under the directive of Mr. Milosevic or Mr. Tudjman, drew the lines, the borders of Bosnia the way they should look in future. This is notoriously untrue. This is a lie. Yes, we did discuss borders. I had this task, but you know in which way: In the event of secession, what would be the situation of the federal units? Would the basis of future borders be the revolutionary outcome or the decisions of the anti-fascist council of Yugoslavia or the organs of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia which decided in the course of the revolution to form six republics and that they should be formed -- or that the borders of these republics should correspond to the divisions and the construction of the Communist Party? That was one of the things that was discussed. Could this be the basis for future borders, which I disputed and said there are just one set of borders which are internationally recognised under multi-lateral contracts concluded after World War I, between 1919 and 1923. The delimitation was finally carried out or effective in 1926 in relation to Albania, but this is not important at the moment. My position was that only these international treaties could be the basis for future borders with which the Croatian side did not agree. My position was that Europe and the world had embarked in a new direction in which the main principle was status quo ante, meaning establishing the situation before the revolution and cancelling out all the things that arisen as a result of the revolution. But these states only had revolutionary legitimacy. They didn't have legal legitimacy because they were not recognised, these borders were not recognised under any international treaties; these are internal borders. So this is a specific position. And this position was regulated in non-legal forms, extra-legal forms. So this is the gist of our discussion during the sessions that we had always in a different location; namely, what would be the basis of future borders? At the time, I referred to the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada, which -- in relation to Quebec, which said that, first of all, Quebec cannot secede unilaterally without the agreement of the rest. Secondly, the borders remain open. So that was the starting position for our negotiations. If --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I just stop you there, because this takes in account another matter that's included within the allegations against Mr. Milosevic. It's been alleged that he was attempting to carve out a Greater Serbia, that his whole policy and strategy was to create this Greater Serbia within the region. Did that accord with any of your instructions with him, discussion was him, or any members of his team? Was that any of your purpose at all?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: No, never. Never. That was not our purpose. I would advise you, gentlemen, there is something that has more weight than what I say and that has more weight than what all of the witnesses say. There are three books. One was written by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. It's called The Islamic Declaration. The second book was written by Mr. Tudjman, where he presented in 500 pages his ideological views and his vision of the future. There is the book of Mr. Milosevic, which was published in 1989, which was translated into French, if I remember. The title of the book is Les Annees Decisives. I think that was the title. Or The Years Of Crisis, in which he presented -- you cannot imagine Mr. Milosevic and his entire framework of ideas unless you place him in the context of that Yugoslavia in which he studied, occupied certain posts, and fervently he -- actually, as far as he was concerned, there was nothing outside of Yugoslavia. In Serbia, even, he was accused of taking too much to heart the slogan introduced after the war, "brotherhood and unity," and he was accused that he was still on that slogan in relation to other nations and nationalities in the country, whereas these people were showing militarist ambitions and aspirations and were in favour of the destruction of the country. Other than that, there is another thing, Mr. Milosevic always cautioned us. And finally, I think, one more thing. I think that is the most important thing: When the terrorist acts, the individual terrorists acts began, I can tell you -- I can describe one which I witnessed. I was there. Following the announcement of the secession by Slovenia, the Slovenian guard killed all the border guards who were on duty at the border. In Yugoslavia, Serb recruits served their military term in Slovenia, Slovenians served their military term in Bosnia; they were all mixed up. When this started to happen, when these first atrocities occurred, Mr. Milosevic was the one who stressed that we had to pacify the public. This was something that was done by individuals. Let us not accuse Slovenia and Slovenes as a whole. Let us not disrupt the relations in Yugoslavia. We must maintain good relations with the other republics. Mr. Milosevic never -- I mean, we cannot even talk about Greater Serbia. You know, for us who lived there, who witnessed all of that, this is something that is ridiculous, to put it mildly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When the conflict started in Slovenia, were you present and discussed what was happening with him and General Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: As I said, the negotiations which were conducted based on -- with this -- this group of Croat intellectuals, we established a very good working relationship. We had meetings in certain places, and then suddenly we -- we were just getting ready. We had been to see Mr. Milosevic when his secretary entered to tell us, no, you are not going - we were getting ready to catch our plane, we were getting ready to go to the airport - Mr. Tudjman has announced that he's suspending all negotiations. That is how it happened. Only later was this commission for negotiations formed, the commission for negotiations with the European Union. And at the invitation of President Milosevic, I was a member of that negotiation team right from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, Professor, just concentrate on answering the question asked by counsel, which was: Were you present and did you discuss what was happening with Mr. Milosevic and General Kadijevic? Just give short answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is exactly what I was going to talk about, but I wanted to explain in which way it happened that I happened to be there. This was a continuing contact that we had, and of course I discussed a lot with Mr. Milosevic, unofficially and officially about these topics. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: If you allow me. I talked with Mr. Kadijevic only when he just happened to come and to report back on certain things or when there was a particular meeting that had to be reported on, but I didn't have independent or direct contacts with Mr. Kadijevic. But he was a member of the delegation, and we always would travel together to The Hague in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But that -- that sets the background, but the issue is really what President Milosevic's attitude was when the conflict in Slovenia started. How did he express his position?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic continued to seek contacts and wanted to continue in any event the negotiations with the Slovenes; namely, when they announced their secession, the Supreme Court of Yugoslavia, the Federal Assembly annulled those contracts or treaties as illegal. However, after Slovenia turned to armed actions against the Yugoslav People's Army, the position of Mr. Milosevic was that we had to negotiate but we have to see, because in my opinion, the borders remain an open question. That was his position. But in any case, to prevent at any cost -- to prevent bloodshed at any cost. That was a very firm position of his. Never -- please. The military or the war option was something that was not considered at that time. If you allow me just one thing: Mr. Milosevic found himself between a rock and a hard place. In Croatia, after these atrocities, because this is something that was not dwelt upon, there were serious atrocities committed against the army in Slovenia, and the extent of that was as follows: There was a series of suicides by high officials because they did not agree with this, and they could not support this. And this is something that is supported by documents. When the instructions -- just one more thing. You overlook the role of Mr. Milosevic. At the time, Mr. Mesic was at the head of the state, and the Prime Minister was Mr. Markovic, also a Croat. So the federal authority was completely in the hands of the Croats. Mr. Milosevic was only in Serbia, in the territory of Serbia, and of course he did have influence to the extent that when they met, the leadership met, he could present the position of Serbia, but he didn't have any decision-making powers. The order to send the army to Slovenia or to send reinforcements to Slovenia was issued by Mr. Markovic as the Prime Minister, but what was tragic was that young people were sent, young recruits who had not had sufficient training, and they did not have any weapons so they were exposed to ruthless destruction in Slovenia. I have a lot of examples. I do not want to burden you with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about the JNA. You've brought that into focus. Because during your discussions with Croatia, had the position and the future of the JNA been a matter for discussion; and what was the position expressed to you and others on your committee of Mr. Milosevic concerning the JNA? What was the policy as expressed to you?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: The position of Mr. Milosevic with respect to the JNA was no different than the position nurtured by each and every Serb, and that was that the army enjoyed enormous authority. That was a tradition. It was the Serb tradition dating back to Turkish times, and the army did enjoy not only authority and respect, deep respect, but Mr. Milosevic had this position and attitude to the army in principle, but of course he was not in command of the army. But, yes, that was the position, it was a position of respect towards it. And even to the present day in Serbia you will come across this attitude on the part of the average Serb citizen. The army, in a way, was untouchable, and thanks to the role that it had during the Balkan wars, the First World War, the Second World War, and so on and so forth, you had this attitude towards it, and that's what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When discussing with the Croatian delegation what was happening, you've told us that the future was even discussed over territorial borders, was the position of the JNA discussed between your delegation and their delegation as to what was to become of it? It was the fourth largest army in Europe at the time.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right, but that's not what we discussed and I'll tell you why straight away, but in order to do so I have to go back once again to our social system. The army was, in a certain sense, decentralised because each federal unit had its own command area, if I can put it that way. And apart from that, along the lines of this ideology of self-management that prevailed, we developed what was called the Territorial Defence, which functioned along the lines of the following slogan: We're all soldiers, we're all there to defend the homeland. That's what was believed. So right down to the local organs, to the grass roots of power and authority, you had territorial units which at any given moment were placed under the command, if the need arose, of the Supreme Command of the army. But we didn't discuss that question at all. We didn't discuss the issue of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We're actually aware of all that background in this courtroom during the last sort of 300 days of evidence. It's the kind of material we've covered, Professor. My question was aimed at whether there was any specific policy put to you by President Milosevic that you were aware of as to what would happen to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We get to the stage, then, on the 25th of June of 1991, when Croatia and Slovenia declared independence and what had been anticipated as a crisis became a reality. Were you in contact with President Milosevic at that time, and if so, are you able to express what his attitude or policy was when that first happened? I'm not dealing in the future now, but at that time when that first happened, were you aware, from discussions with him, as to what his intention was?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I have already said -- or, rather, I can speak about my impressions and the talks I had, the discussions I had. Mr. Milosevic found himself under pressure from two sides. First of all, the mass wave of refugees from Croatia were arriving in Belgrade already at the beginning of July, and the first individual terrorist acts took place in 1990, as early as that. But after the proclamation of the secession, terrorism moved to group terrorism. The reasons for this were multiple: Emigres organisations had moved into Croatia, which were military organisations trained on the territory of, for example, Germany, Australia, and some other countries, and it was common knowledge that the Yugoslavia of the day lodged a series of protests with those countries for having trained and organised terrorist organisations, especially on the territory of Germany, for example, the United States, Canada, and Australia. Germany, for instance, at one point in time, because relations had become tense, really did ban this and disbanded the terrorist camps, training camps that existed at the time. And with the arrival --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, may I interrupt you. The question was a very simple one when you were asked what attitude and intention Mr. Milosevic expressed following on the declarations of independence by Croatia and Slovenia. Now, there must be a simple answer to that question, and if it requires further explanation, no doubt you will give it or Mr. Kay will ask for it, but it would help me greatly if I got an answer to the question first of all before the history that might have led to that answer, because otherwise it's pretty meaningless.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I don't think it is meaningless for the simple reason that you wouldn't be able to understand anything if I gave a yes or no answer, because the situation that existed, that was anarchic, extreme anarchy in the country under the pressure of terrorist acts, you would not be able to understand Mr. Milosevic's attitude and position in a single sentence, but it was we had to negotiate. That is it in a nutshell: We have to negotiate, we have to find a way out of the present situation. Mr. Milosevic at that time addressed the intellectual elite of Serbia, launching appeal and saying that there was a crisis in the country, how can we find a way out of that crisis? We held a series of meetings during that period of time with the aim of finding alternative solutions, and I have here some material which I typed out myself in actual fact on the basis of the conclusions reached at the meetings we held, which were also attended by Mr. Milosevic. Half the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences, university professors, we all attended those meetings. We all rallied together. And none of the people who negotiated at the time with Mr. Milosevic -- actually, he expected much more from us. He expected us to tell him how to find a way out of the situation rather than him telling us. So it's quite an erroneous position if you say that there was just this one personage, this one individual, Mr. Slobodan Milosevic in this case, who made all the decisions. That's not how it was. And I can tell you quite frankly that it was not. You can ask hundreds -- I can assure you that that was the case, and I presented my views, although I never had any political functions, and that's what I told Mr. Milosevic. So I asked him, can I take it upon myself, the responsibility upon myself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So -- so we've moved now to when there is a situation in the former Yugoslavia of Serbian people who are refugees leaving the Croatian republic, as it formerly was, and moving into Serbia, and there are the terrorist acts that you've told us of. Were you thereafter involved as a member in negotiations between the various sides of the territories of the former Yugoslavia from 1991 to 1993?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: No. If you mean in the sense of what we negotiated prior to that on that intellectual level amongst the intellectuals of Serbia and Croatia, then no. But after the secession there was a radical cut, severance, a radical line drawn between the contacts; they were interrupted. So that in Serbia we had the influx of refugees coming in from all sides, and part of the Croatian officials, for example, although many Croats remained in Belgrade - you have 150.000 Croats living in Belgrade and working in different institutions to the present day - but, yes, some white collar workers, officials, did leave Belgrade, those who wished to do so, of course. And on the other hand, you had this terrible pressure from the masses and masses of refugees flowing in, and it became a social problem, how to solve this question of refugees. And Mr. Milosevic was very much involved in these discussions and in finding a solution to the problem. And then you asked me about the contacts. Yes. Up until the formation of the group which was to head the negotiations in The Hague, that is to say here in this city in September, as you well know, 1991, until the end of December, we were here in The Hague, and on the 1st of January, 1992, we relocated to Brussels. Then there was London, and you know the course that these negotiations took afterwards. So up until the formation of that commission we did have contacts which were far more - how should I put this? - on a patriotic basis, that is to say, how to help. My own position, for instance, at the time - and you interrupted me at that point when I was going to tell you this - was the same position taken as many other leading intellectuals regardless of the fact that I wasn't a member of any party. In times of crisis, nobody has the right to remain neutral.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In The Hague on the 7th of September, 1991, when we have the peace conference here, you were a member of the delegation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I wasn't in The Hague on that first day for separate reasons, but I did come later on and came regularly after that. I attended all the meetings after that regularly, but I wasn't there on the 7th of September in The Hague for my own personal reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you were participating, presumably that was as a result of an appointment by President Milosevic or someone else within the Foreign Ministry; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: No. As far as I remember - and Mr. Milosevic will correct me if I'm wrong - it was at the proposal of Mr. Milosevic that the negotiating team was set up and confirmed by the National Assembly, by the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what was the brief you had? What were your instructions as to what you were to seek at the peace conference in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Once again, you will say that I'm going back in time, but you won't be able to understand The Hague without reverting to the Brioni declaration first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just briefly. Just briefly, Professor. You may go back, but just briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, but as I say, you won't be able to understand The Hague without Brioni. The Brioni declaration, first and foremost, the foreign minister, Mr. Loncar at the time, without consulting parliament or the government, invited representatives from the European Union. They did not come to Belgrade, but they did go to Brioni, the Brioni islands. They were invited to come to Brioni, the representatives of all the republics, with the exception of Serbia. Serbia was not present at the Brioni meeting, but there were representatives of the federation present. So in addition to the representatives of the federation, you had the representatives of all the republics except Serbia. Now, when Mr. Jovic who at the time was a member of the Yugoslav state Presidency, so he was there on behalf of the SFRY, representing the SFRY at the Brioni meeting, and he went back to Belgrade, the foreign press wrote about it, the Croatian and Slovenian press wrote about the agreement reached in which the European Union was given the role of mediator. Serbia had absolutely no idea about any of this, and it was faced with a fait accompli, because, first of all, an act of this kind would have to have been ratified by the country's parliament. However, it wasn't brought before parliament at all, and the possibility was that Serbia could revoke this, but it did not do so. And Mr. Jovic made a statement for the press in which he said - and you can find this in his book - no declaration was adopted. They were just talks. That's what he says. It was not ratified at all. However, this draft was conceived as being a definitive solution. And Mr. Milosevic played a key role there at that time. I remember it well. He said, yes, this is contrary to the constitution, but Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond we shall cooperate, and we must place our trust in the European Union or, rather, the European Community, I apologise. It was the European Community at the time. We will accept it regardless of the unlawfulness of the act. We will accept negotiations because there can be no moves forward without negotiations. And I'm now going to state criticism, the criticism I made at the time. I said you're too much of an optimist, and you believe Western diplomacy too much. And those were my words, sir. They were not Mr. Milosevic's words, they were my own words. I said, how can we go forward without any document? And he said, well, we have this one. We analyse the Brioni declaration, and the Brioni declaration, it permits the European Community to find a peaceful solution to the Yugoslav crisis, but with respect for the territorial integrity of Yugoslavia. So it was given the mandate by the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the SFRY, and it was on this basis that we proceeded to negotiate. That is to say we prepared ourselves for the talks, for the negotiations, and I think that the speeches delivered by Mr. Milosevic, which you have before you - I don't want to recount them here and I'm a little taken aback by coming here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tell us now the instructions that you were given as to the line you were to follow at the talks in The Hague, which was the question asked by Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had a platform that we had established, which was adopted unanimously by the Assembly of Serbia. And may I be allowed to remind you that that was a multi-party Assembly at the time. We had already moved to the multi-party system in our political life, and in the Assembly we had seven or eight, I think, parties represented. So this platform was the following: We will go to the negotiations. The borders remain open. If Croatia and Slovenia insist upon seceding, then there is the possibility that Serbia would accept this, but under one condition: That we use peaceful means to decide upon the question of borders, to solve economic problems, and to see about the problem of dual citizenship, because the population was a mixed population and it was no simple matter, and they aspired toward ethnically pure states. So that, then, was the basic premise, and I think perhaps from Mr. Milosevic's speech at the time you will be able to glean that platform of ours as presented by him at the first and second meeting held here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was there any issue that territory would be acquired by military force, that there would be force used to aid --

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- Serbia? You've given evidence about the problem of a large Serbian population being in Croatia, and other republics also had a mix, as we know, and we've had evidence about the figures, of the dispersal of different ethnic groups throughout the territories of the former Yugoslavia. Did Mr. Milosevic express any policy to you in relation to such issues, how those Serbs who were outside the territories of the Republic of Serbia, as it had been, were to be protected or their rights enforced?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: There was a great deal of speculation with the statements made, which, yes, Mr. Milosevic did make I think on two occasions, to the effect that the Serbs should remain and live in one single state. Now, gentlemen, that sentence was pulled out of context. Mr. Milosevic did actually say that, but he also emphasised that, as our constitution speaks about self-determination, including the right to secession under certain conditions, in conformity with all the republics, and so on and so forth, and as self-determination was not a territorial principle in itself, it was the subjective right of peoples as such, not the territorial principle. So it was impossible to have self-determination of the federal units. Where would the logic of that be? There is no link between the substance of self-determination, especially as defined by the General Assembly. And you know full well, or let me remind you - I don't think I have to do so, though - of the Resolutions of the General Assembly which clearly state that self-determination and secession are two separate legal acts. And this was confirmed by the International Court of Law, for example, that secession was not linked or need not necessarily be linked to self determination as a legal principle and secession as a political one, and the International Court of Justice ruled that way with respect to Sahara. So we were of that view. It was not a territorial principle, it was the subjective principle of a people. So the Serbs as a core, as a constituent nation, had the right to self-determination. Now, what logic would you apply if you had to divide up this Serbian entity? There would be no logic either to be found in law or as a precedent at all. So it was along those lines and in that sense that Mr. Milosevic and not only Mr. Milosevic but the Presidency, the federal Yugoslav state Presidency itself expressed and told the Serbs that they would have protection, enjoy protection. And the president of the Yugoslav state Presidency himself - and we had the principle of rotation for the Presidency president, at the time it was Mr. Kostic who was present - and I remember this well and I quote him in my books, he said the following, because you know Mr. Milosevic strove and accepted the arrival of the international forces. The Serbs in Croatia did not accept that for the simple reason that they said, well, we don't need any foreign troops. We had what you said a moment ago, one of the strongest armies. So why should not our army protect the people and introduce law and order into the country? Why would we need international forces to do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Moving on to other issues here, and I want to try to keep it in a chronology, we've mentioned the Hague in September --

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Please. It is not -- it was not clearly -- stated clearly enough, that is to say the grounds upon which Mr. Milosevic wanted to assure the Serbs. I have a document here. I hope it's been translated, but these are the variations, that is to say the different ways and means in which the Serb question in Croatia could be solved. Now, these variants were compiled on the basis of broad consultations held among intellectuals, professionals of all profiles. So the war option was excluded. Without too much modesty I will have to say that I am the author. I wrote this for the most part, but it was compiled on the basis of the discussions held in Mr. Milosevic's offices, in his cabinet. And I can tell you who was present, all the academicians, the professors who attended that meeting, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I could see that document and see whether there is a copy before us.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: This is the original typed out by me personally. I didn't have a computer, so I had to type it out on an ordinary typewriter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I could just retain this and in the break have a look at it and maybe --

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- seek to get it copied, that meeting be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the benefit of transcript, the Presiding Judge asked who was the author. It should be at line 38. Yes, please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we're reaching a convenient moment here, Your Honour, before I move on to the declaration of independence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay. The Professor, in my estimation, has evidence to give relevant to the issues in this case, but it would be more profitable, I think, if the questioning were more direct and the answers much shorter. Professor, I appreciate that you want to provide a background to the answers and that, in your view, would better enable us to understand the issues, but you must try as best as you can to answer the questions directly. There is within this Tribunal, I think, two ways of giving evidence. One is the narrative approach, which is more common in the inquisitorial system, and in the common law tradition from which I come questions are put directly and answers given. We have to strike a balance in relation to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will take the adjournment now. Professor, in the adjournment, which will be for 20 minutes, you are not to discuss your evidence with anybody. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the adjournment, copies have been produced of the document, Professor Avramov, that you showed us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The Prosecution already have copies of these, Your Honour, and so does Mr. Milosevic. If you could hand that back to the witness and then those are for the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position about this exhibit, as with the small clutch of exhibits provided a few days ago in respect of this witness, is that none of the B/C/S versions has been translated, and I have not in the event been in a position to deal with this document in any detail at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It seems to be a very short document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, fairly short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What do you intend to do with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I was going to get the witness to identify the document, tell us in summary form what it says and how it is relevant rather than read it all out, and the translation then can be produced if that is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Professor Avramov, this is the document you referred to just before the break when you gave evidence, and you told us that you typed this document in 1991; is that right? And was that June?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: June 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I think so, yes. June or July. I can't remember exactly now. Perhaps I put the date somewhere. No. No, I didn't. I didn't put the date anywhere. But you see, I would like to point something out to you once again, that this was the result of our discussions with -- with the representatives, with the representatives of the Serbs from Croatia and this circle of intellectuals gathered around Mr. Milosevic in order to assist him at that moment. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is this a summary of the negotiations between your committee and the committee that was representing Croatia in that period from March until the summer of 1991?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes. Representatives from Croatia did take part in this. That explains the context, I repeat. For example, Variant 1: Croats totally leave Yugoslavia with part of the territory of present-day Croatia. Serb areas in Croatia remain in Yugoslavia on the basis of the right of people to self-determination. All questions related to the Croats leaving Yugoslavia shall be regulated by way of agreement between the Croatian authorities and the organs of Yugoslavia. Variant number 2: Croats gradually and within a certain transition period leave Yugoslavia, however remaining a certain relationship with Yugoslavia whose substance level of links and dynamics shall be established by way of agreement between Croatian organs and the organs of Yugoslavia. And also another very important one: Serb territories shall determine their status through a constitutional document during the transition period with the agreement of the Croatian authorities and the organs of Yugoslavia, and the implementation of this enactment shall be guaranteed by the international community through an international agreement. On the territories of the Serb territories, there cannot be any armed forces of the Republic of Croatia or of Yugoslavia, and the territory can have its own police forces needed for the protection of citizens from crime and in order to maintain public law and order. And this enactment would probably relate only to the economy in order to divide the jurisdiction involved. Where the regulations of the republics of Croatia and Yugoslavia will be implemented, the regulations of the organs of Yugoslavia will be implemented. So it's a kind of combination. Authority in all regulations and all fields in the first degree shall be carried out by the organs of the independent territory and in the second degree in the areas in which the Republic of Croatia maintains relations with Yugoslavia shall be resolved by the organs of Croatia, rather, the organs of Yugoslavia, depending on the agreement on mutual relations. Representatives of the independent territories shall be present in an appropriate manner in the organs of the Republic of Croatia and in the organs of Yugoslavia as well, in accordance with the areas in which there are mutual relations. All controversial questions in the implementation of mutual relations in the territory of the independent territory shall be resolved by a commission consisting of representatives of the organs of the independent territories of the organ of Croatia, the organ of Yugoslavia, and the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's sometimes difficult for me to cut off the witness because I have to let the translation go on and I don't come over that, so it does make it difficult controlling in those circumstances. I hope the Court understands that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I'm doing my best in relation to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This document, then, was drafted by you at a stage when you were thinking of the future and that if Croatia did secede that what would be remaining would still be a Yugoslavia but without Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: That was the basic problem in our negotiations here in The Hague on the 18th of October, 1991. And if you permit me to say so, that is precisely where we broke off. The Brioni declaration gives the representatives of the European Community the mandate to negotiate and mediate, however maintaining the territorial integrity of Yugoslavia. However, on the 18th of October, without any preparations, without any previous information, I was informed 24 hours beforehand. We received the so-called Carrington paper which puts to us the disintegration of Yugoslavia without any alternatives. There would be no negotiations. What we expected on the Brioni declaration was not to be. This is an ultimatum. There are no negotiations to accept or reject. There is no third option. And to everyone's astonishment, they accepted revolutionary principles, you see. They accepted states within the borders that were established during the revolution, the AVNOJ borders, which was unacceptable for us. I have to remind you that the borders of Yugoslavia after the Second World War were regulated by many-fold treaties concluded then by Yugoslavia or, rather, Serbia. Serbia was the only state that was entitled to negotiate after the First World War. This was the First World War. So all of this came into force after the Second World War to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I can just stop you there, with my apologies. The position then with the Carrington Plan had not been what your delegation had had in mind for what it saw then as the future of Yugoslavia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: No. At that time, after having come to the conclusion that Croatia and Slovenia were categorically in favour of leaving Yugoslavia, that was the idea of President Milosevic, and he presented that idea. There was a big discussion in Belgrade when he presented that concept of his: All right, we are not going to oppose this. Let us not allow a war to take place in the territory. Croatia and Slovenia will go their own way whereas those peoples who wish to remain within Yugoslavia will remain within this future smaller Yugoslavia. The point was in the following, in what Mr. Milosevic said, that is: There cannot be a right -- the right to secession cannot be stronger, cannot supersede the right to the integrity of the state. This was my reaction or, rather, President Milosevic's reaction after we read the paper, the Carrington paper; that this was a pure deception, because it deviated from the Brioni declaration. He had received his mandate from Yugoslavia, not the republics, and this is what President Milosevic said in his speech on the 18th of October, 1991. That's what he highlighted: We are not opposed to them going their own way, but the final say has to be that of the people themselves. A representative or an envoy who got a certain mandate, a restricted mandate, cannot decide on the dissolution -- dissolution of Yugoslavia, as he called it. It is not a dissolution. Even Lord Carrington himself and others later realised that this led to bloodshed and also an aggravation of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At this time in 1991, was it any part of President Milosevic's policy to expel any of those of different ethnic groups from the Serbs from the territories of Yugoslavia as he envisaged it as being, or from the territories of Serbia, for that matter? Was there any question of the expulsion of people that you know of within his policy?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Never. Gentlemen, it is not only that Serbs were the refugees who were coming in. Do you want me to give you the names of famous Croatian writers who found refuge in Serbia in 1991? Also, thousands of Albanians fled from Kosovo under the terror there, from the terror there, and came to Serbia. There were federal officials who voluntarily left with their own belongings on trucks. However, we had officers who were coming back to Belgrade or, rather, I'm sorry, families of officers who were expelled from their own apartments and they were not allowed to take along even their personal belongings. So this caused revolt in Serbia, because it was obvious, as it was shown on television, when Slovenian recruits were leaving, they were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, you have answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You've told us that President Milosevic, on the 18th of October, recognised, after Croatia on the 8th of October had declared independence, that they were going their own way. Was his view supported politically within Yugoslavia or were there others in opposition to his view of acceptance of what had happened with Slovenia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Of course there were very many. You have to realise that we had tens of thousands of mixed marriages. There were people who were truly oriented towards a feeling of Yugoslavia. They are living harbouring these ideas until the present day. They cannot think otherwise. They even write books. They are called -- it is called Yugo-nostalgia. That's what the feeling is called. On our way back from here, on the plane at that time, we had representatives of the military there, and there was Mr. Milosevic, and Mr. Bulatovic and all of us who took part in the conference at that time, and we call came to the conclusion that the Carrington paper was a watershed, that it was a turning point in the negotiations, and that our refusal to accept the Carrington paper -- because we resolutely refused to accept it and that is what Mr. Milosevic said, it is only the people who can reach this kind of a decision, not the mediator himself. This is in accordance with national and international law. We talked on the plane, and we came to the conclusion - I think this was the initiative of Mr. Milosevic himself - to convene an extraordinary session of the parliament where the Carrington paper would be presented and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor. Professor --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Federal Assembly, as the highest organ of the people, should express its views on whether they are in favour of President Milosevic's position or not. That night an extraordinary session of the parliament was held, and this expression expounded by Mr. Milosevic in The Hague was adopted unanimously by parliament. It was even the opposition parties that voted in favour of that, and the representative of the strongest opposition party, who is today the foreign minister of Yugoslavia, said quite literally, "Mr. President, had you acted otherwise, I would have accused you as a traitor today."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: From what you're saying, Mr. Milosevic had to consider the other issues within Serbia, the other republics, as to their interests, what was in the best interests of what remained of Yugoslavia with those two republics having seceded. Was there any policy that you were aware of that he wanted to use force whilst negotiations were continuing, whilst peace plans were being discussed, as a way of imposing pressure on the newly declared State of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: No. Gentlemen, I have this here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the documents here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, just a minute. Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, all these questions that have been put so far by Mr. Kay are absolutely out of line in terms of the concept of my defence, and they are, as a matter of fact, in total contrast to the line of defence that I had prepared. I believe that this is due to his lack of knowledge. And also, I think that this is done in order to dilute the statement of the witness. You turned off my microphone, I did not manage to switch off my microphone. It is not true what Mr. Kay said, that through someone I asked him to say here -- or, rather, request that I question the witness first. I actually have no intention of exercising any rights as Mr. Kay's assistant. I'm not going to accept that, exercising my right to defence in that way, that is to say depending on your mercy, that you are just giving me crumbs of that right and in that way I am going to exercise my right to defence. So I ask you that you return my right of defence to me because it is quite clear to everyone that what Mr. Kay is doing here does not constitute my defence and does not constitute the exercise of my right to defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. Mr. Milosevic, let me say firstly that the questions asked by Mr. Kay are, in the view of the Chamber, relevant to the issues in this case. They go to your state of mind, to the question of individual criminal responsibility. Let me say secondly that in line with the order made by the Chamber, you may be allowed to ask additional questions. That's a matter that the Chamber will consider on a case-by-case basis. Mr. Kay, proceed with the examination. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On that note, may I say something in relation to what Mr. Milosevic raised just now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly. Mr. President, I accepted to be a witness in this trial, although I had left the negotiating team due to certain differences and divergences, but I believe that giving evidence, giving testimony is an ethical category. I was motivated only by a wish to contribute to an extremely complicated case, as is the case of the destruction of Yugoslavia and the role of Mr. Milosevic in this entire case. But much more than that, this is not only in the interest of Mr. Milosevic. It is in the interest of the country. It is in the interest of the people that I belong to. But I may I say at this point in time that this is primarily in the interest of the science of law, which is facing one of the gravest crises in its history. I started studying law in 1936 in Vienna, and those were the years of a grave crisis, and this crisis is far graver than that one as far as law is concerned. So I thought that in this way there would be a rehabilitation, so to speak, by way of presenting the proof -- the truth, that is, there would be a rehabilitation of legal order and the rule of law. According to your rules, a witness has to be prepared and has to have contact with the Defence, in this specific case it was Mr. Milosevic. Thanks to your approval and permission, I had meetings with him and we chronologically went from one stage to another, how things developed for as long as I was on the negotiating team. I happened to meet Mr. Kay only yesterday, so I did not have contact with him before, only with Milosevic. Allow me to speak as a lawyer now with 60 years of professional experience in the legal profession. I have devoted my entire life to that profession and my entire career. The right to defence belongs to the category of ius cogens --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you on that. I'm stopping you on that, Professor. I'm stopping you on that. That's not a matter for you to discuss now. Mr. Kay, you may proceed with your examination. And please answer the questions that are asked as directly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The question I asked, Professor Avramov, was this: Was there any policy, after Croatia had declared independence on the 8th of October, 1991, that Mr. Milosevic had directed the JNA or paramilitaries to use force against the declared territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Sir, I used to spend the entire day at the Presidency at that time. Mr. Milosevic did not have any influence over the JNA. You have to be aware of the way in which paramilitary forces were being established, the way in which the Serb people spontaneously rose against violence. Please. I gave you this order as an example, and there were so many. This is a photocopy of the original poster that will be shown at the military museum in Belgrade. It will be an exhibit there. This is the order of the Crisis Staff of Croatia that within 48 hours, 25 big Serb settlements in Slavonia should be emptied. They were ordered where they were supposed to gather collectively. If they do not do so, they will be severely punished. Bearing in mind that the genocide in 1941 started in those same areas in a very similar way, this is the most densely populated Serb area, these 25 villages, and this was carried by the newspapers. There were posters all over with this order. And Serbs boarded their tractors, their wagons, and 30.000 or 40.000 of them left and arrived in Belgrade. Others who did not want to leave their houses were killed and --
