utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, I'm stopping you. Mr. Kay, next question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But how was this established, sir? How was this established, this third part that did not wish to flee, that did not wish to surrender? They went into the woods. They rebelled. And those were the first groups of resistance against violence, against violence, which irritated the population everywhere. And there were even volunteers in Serbia who made themselves available to the Yugoslav People's Army. What you have to know in addition to that is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We've had your explanation. Next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: May I ask the professor a question at this stage? Professor, Professor Avramov --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why will you not answer the question you've just been asked which was about the attitude, intention of Mr. Milosevic at that time? Why do you have to tell us about what the attitude of Croatians were at that time? Can you not please direct your mind to the questions you're being asked, which are plainly in the interests of Mr. Milosevic and which you plainly are apparently not willing to answer directly. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot respond more directly than I did. Mr. Milosevic did not have a position at the time about what to do with the mass of refugees and with the organised group in Croatia over which he had no influence. And these groups of Serbs had formed on their own initiative in self-defence. Mr. Milosevic had nothing to do with that. I perhaps had more contact with them because I was a member of humanitarian organisations, so I knew much more than Mr. Milosevic did about that. He just was caught in the situation. At that point, he did not have any influence in that area. Mr. Mesic and Mr. Markovic had influence instead of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Professor, you referred to a document there which I've got copies of. It's a number DPH 984, and it's got the figure 1 on it that has been supplied to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I could just hand this document around. The Prosecution already have it already at DPH 984. There are copies here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This document, it's a document we've seen, we haven't had a translation, but it may be appropriate to get from the witness more evidence of its provenance before it's admitted into evidence. I don't know what she's saying about it. It's clearly a document that could be typed by anyone in any circumstances, and we need to know what she's saying about whether and where she found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will obviously be doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We're looking at this document now. We've all got it, Professor. First of all, can you tell us where the document came from. How have you got this document? Where did you obtain it from?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: The document which the refugees brought with them, the ones who arrived, you can see these lines here. When I got this original, the document was crumpled up because it was in the pocket of one of the refugees. We straightened it and made a copy, and then you can see what kind of a copy it is. The document was published in the Croatian press, in the Slavonski Glasnik, a local Pozega paper. This document was posted on all corners, on all notice boards in these villages which were supposed to be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did you get a copy of this document?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: In September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And were you in Belgrade at that time?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the document, you said, was with a refugee. Can you tell us what it actually says on it in summary form. What does it declare?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: The citizens will move out to the populated area of the Slavonska Pozega municipality according to their free choice. Those who have no place to shelter themselves are obliged to contact the relief teams of the civilian protection for evacuation in the areas in the collection areas of Ivandol, Dezevci, Perenci, Toranj, and Biskupci. This order goes into effect on the 29th of October, 1991, at 12.00, and the decision will be in force depending on when the situation in the area calms down. When the deadline for the -- for the population to remove them -- to leave, any movement of civilians in the cited area will be banned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And who is this document aimed at? Who is it telling to evacuate?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: You can see what the introductory part says. I just read the body of the message. I quote: "Recently the Chetnik terrorist forces and units of the JNA have been threatening with their activities the civilian population in the western part of Slavonska Pozega, so for the purpose of protecting their lives and making it possible for our defence forces in that area to conduct a defence, the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Slavonska Pozega announces that all citizens should evacuate with their personal property, food articles, clothing, footwear, sheets, personnel hygiene items," and so on, and then they mention the names of the villages or the places that are to be evacuated - I don't need to read all of them - "within 48 hours from the time when this order goes into effect." That means that they had to leave their houses within 48 hours and report to the collection sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the citizen that you obtained this from, what ethnic group was he?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Serbs. Serb refugees who came.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the villages that are named here, were they villages containing mainly Serb people?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Exclusively Serbs. These were Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So I go back to the main issue here which we're dealing with in October 1991, because there are allegations concerning the bombardment of Dubrovnik, the area around Dubrovnik, conflict in the Krajina, whether as far as you knew that was the policy and declared intent of Mr. Milosevic, that there should be attacks on Croatia as a way of forcing pressure on Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: No. Again you will say that I'm going back, but it is impossible to respond with a yes or no. But if you want me to respond with a yes or no, then I say no, that was not his order. But I have to say when the secession happened, representatives of the Serbian people came to Belgrade and demanded forcefully to be protected by Yugoslavia, the only legitimate representative in the international community, the only subject in the international community. They expressed the desire to be protected and to remain within Yugoslavia. Mr. Milosevic and the Serbian government provided assurances to them that they would do everything to protect them. You have the daily newspapers' reports, you have the daily government statements and statements of President Milosevic to this effect. However, since the terrorist acts which had grown into mass crimes continued, Serbs in Croatia charged or accused Belgrade of not providing adequate protection to them and that they would be forced to defend themselves. So when it was suggested to them that President Milosevic launches an initiative for the Assembly to declare that those areas never seceded, namely that they remained, which is a fact, the sovereignty of Croatia in that area was not established until 1995, until the well-known Storm offensive, because the Territorial Defence was in the hands of the Serbs in that area. They were armed through the Territorial Defence. So they organised self-defence. In their deep disappointment - I repeat deeply disappointed - with the position of Belgrade and us who were there because we had not offered them adequate protection. And in that period, these clashes confirmed -- occurred. As far as July, don't forget that in July there was a proposal, and later this became an order, that members of the JNA should withdraw to their barracks, which they did. They obeyed that order. And the army found itself closed in its own barracks, which were then surrounded by paramilitary forces. This happened in Slovenia and in Croatia. Their electricity and water were cut off, and there was mass -- there were mass deaths within the barracks as well as mass rebellions there. I cited several examples of this in my book, and I also have many documents from that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kay, next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: From 1991, we move to 1992, and on the 15th of January, 1992, the European Community recognised Croatia as an independent state. Did you have any discussions with President Milosevic as to the effect of that recognition by the European Community in January 1992?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: The recognition was heralded in the international press already as early as June 1991. There's an interview by Mr. Genscher from that period in which he said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have to stop you. Just answer the question. The question is: Did you have any discussions with President Milosevic as to the effect of that recognition by the European Community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We talked before that also because the National Assembly, following the announcement of the recognition, the Federal Assembly sent a protest to the United Nations and to the European Union that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm stopping you there. The answer is yes. Mr. Kay, do you want to follow up on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Had there been any discussions as to the effect, politically, of what was now taking place upon Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I will tell you. Mr. Milosevic asked me a specific question when we were talking about this, and he asked me, from an international standpoint, how can you qualify recognition today? My answer was based on the discussion of the General Assembly of the United Nations when the Resolution was adopted in which the term of aggression was defined, is that recognition is an indirect form aggression against the SFRY. That was my response to Mr. Milosevic and to the whole group of negotiators who participated in that. The effect was horrible, the effect of that move, because all the masks were dropped, all pretense was dropped on behalf of the -- on the part of the negotiating team and the international community. You know, that's a euphemism, the international community. We did not deal with the international community but the representatives of the international community and the representatives of the United States. The "international community" is a wider, broader term. So this recognition was a -- caused a considerable amount of shock, this recognition did. And there was -- if you allow me. You asked me whether I talked with him. Yes, I did, before that. But on the 15th of January, I happened to be in Brussels together with a group which was supposed to take part in different -- in work of different expert teams, and because we flew in, you know that Serbia was isolated and we could not have any contacts, we were consulting each other about what to do next. With the recognition, the European Union lost its right to mediate. So without the knowledge of Mr. Milosevic, on our own initiative, again I would like to show you an act which I wrote in the hotel room. It's written in English. Perhaps the English is not that good, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm actually interested here in Mr. Milosevic's reaction as you were to see it. What policy were you aware of that he was in mind as a result of the Bosnian fear that they would form a separate republic as well?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: This was the Carrington paper already. It was an ultimatum. All the republics would acquire independence, and they would have the right to request recognition from the international community, as they called it. There was no alternative to that. We gave several amendments to that paper which were not accepted. We had a central idea in all of these amendments. We thought, all right, very well, secession of Slovenia and Croatia, but you cannot dispute that those who wished to remain within Yugoslavia remain there. At that time, the war did not break out, so those who wished to remain in Yugoslavia could do so. That was our amendment. However, Lord Carrington and the others who were there were categorical in their answer: No, they wanted the break-up, total fragmentation of Yugoslavia, which was something we could not accept. So then when this was being discussed, because the Yugoslav army was closed off in its barracks and the paramilitary forces of Slovenia and Croatia had full freedom of movement, they had surrounded the barracks, they were attacking and killing, then an order was issued, not by President Milosevic but by -- not by Mr. Milosevic but by the Supreme Command that these barracks should be set free, they should be deblocked. And this is where a broader clash occurred between the JNA and the paramilitary forces of Slovenia and Croatia, and even Bosnia, because under the order of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic in Sarajevo, even though the war had not broken out there, the barracks were blockaded there as well. There were military schools there, and these military schools were surrounded. These schools were attended by young men who were not of age yet, so these places were attacked then. The army went into action in order to free those barracks, and that is when these conflicts occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware of any policy by President Milosevic of cleansing areas of people so that they would only have Serbs residing in them, such as in the Krajina or in Bosnia? Was that -- did that form any part of the policy or planning in your daily meetings with him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And just a simple, direct answer to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Absolutely there were no such ideas at all. I don't know how you came to that. I was present. I participated in that. What I can reproach him with is that Mr. Milosevic was obsessed with the slogan "brotherhood and unity," and let's preserve what can be preserved. Please. Not a single Croat was harmed. Not a hair on their head was harmed in Serbia. They are still living there today. Serbia remains to be a multi-ethnic unit out of all the other republics in Yugoslavia, the only one such unit. But I could reproach Mr. Milosevic in this aspect, and he was quite strongly criticised for this position in Serbia also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The JNA that we've discussed earlier, at that time in 1992, after European Community recognition of Croatia, are you able to tell us what policy President Milosevic had in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I told you that there was resistance primarily on the part of the Federal Assembly, then the Assembly of Serbia. They lodged a protest against recognition in the belief that this was direct interference in the internal affairs of Yugoslavia, that this was an act of indirect aggression against Yugoslavia. The reaction of Mr. Milosevic and, I would say, the entire Serbian public was negative, which was later affirmed, because as you know, and everyone confirmed that later in their memoirs that this was the biggest mistake that was made in the process of dealing with Yugoslavia, this recognition that this caused, and this is, amongst other things, something that I think Lord Owen said. He devoted a few -- several pages to this topic in his book. You can also take the views of general -- the UNPROFOR generals in Croatia or of Mr. Stoltenberg. I have many of these statements where it is said that they thought this was a catastrophic mistake and that everybody was horrified because of this move. But if you allow me just one explanation now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you can deal with this issue, which is that in March 1992, we have the conflict starting in Bosnia, and it's -- it is the role that paramilitaries or JNA forces were to have in that conflict as a matter of policy. Do you know what President Milosevic was planning, what he was doing? What was his policy? What did he talk to you about?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic accepted the order of the Supreme Command, the withdrawal of the JNA to Serbia. However, during the withdrawal - you know the massacres that occurred in Tuzla, in Sarajevo, and so on and so forth - but in this withdrawal, in view of the fact that the JNA comprised officers from various parts of the country because a lot of attention was paid to keep a balance or an equilibrium in the military units, so that those who were from Serbia or soldiers or officers who were from Croatia simply did not wish to withdraw. They stayed in their homes. The same thing happened in Bosnia. They stayed in their homes. So those who wanted to, withdrew to Serbia, and these were mostly people who were born in Serbia, who lived there and had their families there and belonged there. As far as the others were concerned, the majority of them stayed where they were. Mr. Milosevic, or President Milosevic at the time, was following and accepting the decisions of the Supreme Command. He didn't command. The Command issued the order to withdraw following the deblocking of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was there any policy that he had that you were aware of that he -- that supported the use of force from Serbia, either by paramilitaries or the JNA, to take control of territory in Bosnia or Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: No. I state categorically no. You can see this best through the correspondence of Mr. Milosevic with representatives of the government of the Serbian Krajina or Republika Srpska, so with Mr. Martic, Karadzic, with all of these members of that government, and I took part in that as well. There was a constant clash taking place in these contacts because he continually wanted to increase the engagement of Serbia. Mr. Milosevic said, "Well, wait. We have to coordinate things with the international community." He was trying to persuade or convince the Serbs and was trying to calm down the situation in a way. On one occasion I was listening to Mr. Babic when he was testifying, yes, but I happened to be present during the same events, and it is not true what he testified. I was present at a meeting when Mr. President -- when Mr. Milosevic asked me -- let me just tell you, representatives of Republika Srpska and the Serbian Krajina did not take part in the negotiations until the beginning of 1992. We were the ones who were representing their interests. But at the same time, we fought and strived to enable the representatives of the Krajina and the representatives of Serbs from Bosnia and Herzegovina to defend their own interests there. And that is how it came about that they were included in the negotiating teams. So Mr. Milosevic, at that meeting, asked me to tell the gentleman from Knin how far we had gotten in the negotiations to date, how we felt we should proceed further and what was the European Union's vision of the development of the situation. After two sentences of mine, Mr. Martic -- no, Mr. Babic, excuse me -- interrupted me and he said to Mr. Milosevic, "We did not come here to listen to you, to see what you did and what you did not do. We came here to tell you what we want, and we will not accept any of your decisions if they are adopted against our will." That was their position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As you told us, in January of 1992 there was the Brussels conference, and then in August of 1992 there is the conference at London. Again, you're still part of the negotiating team?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was the object of your negotiations, from instructions by Mr. Milosevic, to achieve peace or to stall and obstruct and cause problems? What was it?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: No. He insisted upon the speediest possible solution by peaceful means. And you have the minutes, you have the records that were kept by the European Community, or the records and minutes that were kept in London. And I recorded the meetings for myself, for my own purposes, on Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond that occasion. So you have the minutes. You have their records on the position taken by Mr. Milosevic, and that is much more authentic than anything I can tell you here. No, he had no ideas of any violent solutions. He was fully conscious, fully aware of the situation that he faced and was looking for assistance, help in saving what could be saved, salvaging what there was to salvage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did he ever express to you how the international community could have supported him to achieve peace, how their policy could have helped him more? Did he ever express to you?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: Our views diverged there, and that was the reason why we parted ways. Mr. Milosevic kept insisting, regardless of what we had experienced from the so-called international community, that we had to pursue the negotiations, to continue them because they were our former allies, he said, and we will, I'm sure, arrive at a point upon which we agree. There is no other way out for us except to negotiate and negotiate with the West until a solution is found. My position was that we must draw a line somewhere and say, gentlemen, that's as far as we'll go. And that's what I wrote down. We were duped by the European Union, we are going to interrupt negotiations with you, and we're going to step down from the United Nations. I said that to Mr. Milosevic once in 1992, and he didn't accept it. So he was highly cooperative, in fact, during those negotiations, cooperative in the sense that he was always interested in the intentions of the European Community representatives, but we criticised him at home because we thought that he was going too far in relaxing before the international community, to the detriment of the interests of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It was felt that there were nations within Europe who had actively worked for the break-up of Yugoslavia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: That was not an assumption. Those were facts, gentlemen. We had the numbers of accounts in Swiss banks that our services, our security service or whatever supplied us with, and the firms, the companies through which arms reached the paramilitaries in Croatia, Slovenia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, for instance. Those are the facts. That is one point. Now, secondly, you also have statements by --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I can stop you there. There was a body of evidence that you and others had seen, and that no doubt President Milosevic had seen, concerning activities of European states in relation to acknowledging Croatia, supporting Croatia, Slovenia. Was his position on this viewed by the rest of you as being strong or weak, or was he taking a position of negotiation that many others did not support?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: In Serbia, many did not support him because he thought -- they thought he was yielding too much and accommodating, being accommodating. They considered that President Milosevic was going too far in this accommodation, because any -- all the demands he met didn't have the desired result. It didn't lead to an end to the problem but new ultimatums, new requests, and that's how it went to the present day, further and further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you also involved in the Cutileiro plan, which came about after Lord Carrington's plan?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I understand. Well, I was kept abreast, but I wasn't actually involved. There was another team that went and attended those negotiations. After they were given the status of negotiator, a team from Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina went and set up their own teams that went, so that in actual fact I was not among them. They were the representatives or, rather, I know that President Karadzic led a delegation of Republika Srpska, and with him he had a team. I think they're on the list of -- the witness list, those people who went and who were members. I wasn't there, but I was, of course, kept abreast, and I received all the material facts to Belgrade on developments at the negotiations, how Cutileiro's plan was evolving, and I had all the documents with me, yes, I did, in my hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You told us that in 1993, you actually ceased your involvement for President Milosevic and the government in relation to the --

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- negotiations and peace processes. And what was the reason for you ceasing to be involved, and what date was that when you stopped your active participation?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I couldn't actually give you an exact date, but yes, it was the beginning of April 1993. And the reasons are readily understandable. I have made them public. We had our position of principle, and that was that the borders remained an open problem. We did not recognise the AVNOJ anti-fascist borders known as the AVNOJ, but President Milosevic considered that the negotiations should be continued and this should be accepted as a sort of fait accompli. So he did continue the negotiations, and this was one of the reasons for which we did not see -- on which we did not see eye-to-eye. And a moment ago, as I told you, I myself considered that we had experienced the greatest deception on the part of the international community. And I told Mr. Milosevic that as a legal person myself I did not want to bear the historical responsibility for that nor did I want to be a member of the team who took that upon itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what was his commitment still then in 1993 when you withdrew?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Always the same position, always the same commitment: Let us continue the negotiations with the West. We have no alternative. They are our historical allies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just on other matters now. You've mentioned Babic. You've mentioned -- I don't think you've mentioned Martic yet, but what I want to ask you questions about now is Mr. Milosevic's influence over others who are involved in events that took place. Were you able to see, for instance, what influence, what sort of relationship he had with Babic?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Babic was an individual, a personage who was a little extravagant, very convinced of his own potential, very self-confident and self-assured and saw himself as a statesman and leader, and as such he did not allow anybody to wield any influence on him. He would always reject all proposals very radically. So those links, those ties, were never coordinated or harmonised, and it wasn't the kind of cooperation that one should feel should have been present between individuals negotiating within a circle of people and upon whom the fate of the nation rested. And Mr. Martic was far more cooperative, quite a different personage, had quite a different character to Mr. Babic. But the Republika Srpska Krajina had its own parliament, as you know, its own government, and you couldn't wield any influence outside the decisions taken by that very same government. So during the war, I myself on several occasions went to Pale and to Knin, and I attended one occasion when there was a meeting held in Knin. This is how it was: You know, those people there felt themselves to be under jeopardy. They thought that they had been played out by the party and army and government, and they felt that they had to rely on their own forces alone, and this added to their sense of -- can I say sense of pride or whatever. I can't find the right terms to express the feeling.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This can be looked at in two ways. Firstly, did they think that Mr. Milosevic was doing enough to support them? Did they think he should be doing more? Did they think that he was giving sufficient support?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: No. They considered that not only Mr. Milosevic but, generally speaking, that Serbia hadn't done enough for them. And that's what they told me. They told me that just as they told other people. I was not an important member of the team, but they told me nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The other side of looking at it is the impact on the peace negotiations, conferences that you were involved with for Mr. Milosevic. How easy was it for him and for you and others to negotiate and deal in relation to the set-up in the RSK?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: It was extremely difficult, extremely difficult. It's a subject that I have engaged in scientific research in for a long time and am still doing now, what the background was and what the reasons were and why our former allies took this position, this hostile position, to Serbia and did not show understanding for the tragic position in which the Serb people found themselves. This is something that for me personally still remains unclear. I am not sufficiently cognisant of the reasons, although in looking through documents that have come my way I have gleaned the reasons, but we were in a very unfavourable situation. We did not have any support. We were faced from the very beginning, from Carrington's document, with an ultimatum, one ultimatum after another. There were no alternatives. Take it or leave it; that was the principle that prevailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Politically, were you able to see if that caused President Milosevic difficulties in dealing with the politicians back in Serbia? What effect did that have?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes, it did have an effect, an enormous effect, and it made it much more difficult. And Mr. Milosevic found himself between a rock and a hard place, in between political parties, one that had a weaker position or one that had a stronger position vis-a-vis the situation. So, yes, it did make it significantly more difficult. Mr. Milosevic's position was made significantly more difficult, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I want to now turn that issue to look at Bosnia and Radovan Karadzic, who was the leader of the Bosnian Serbs. Are you able to say from what you were able to see and observe what influence Mr. Milosevic had over Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Well, you know, Mr. Karadzic, and unfortunately those of them who have died in the meantime, they were all intellectuals with high moral integrity, and they always posed themselves on a horizontal plane and not on a vertical plane. Mr. Karadzic was highly respected as an individual, not only as an exceptional neuropsychiatrist, a very well known professional who had published many works in the field, and the fact that he took the side of his people in the most difficult times, which shot up his rating in those circles. He was a very forceful personality, a strong character who, as I've already said, put himself on a footing of equality when discussing with -- when discussing with -- matters with others, with Mr. Milosevic. Only it was with a heavy heart that he gave up directly negotiating at Dayton and leaving that role of negotiator up to Mr. Milosevic. But that was the requirement that had been made by the European Community, as you know full well. And Mr. Milosevic there played a very -- the role of a virtuoso. He had to convince him and them to be the representative, the sole representative, in actual fact, of all the parties in the conflict. Those were some exceptionally difficult times. If you were to look at the press in our country dating back to those times, which was full of criticisms, attacks, acquiescence and criticism. It was a highly tense situation. Some people approved, others didn't. That was what it was like. However, I have to say, and you know full well, how Cutileiro's plan came about in the first place, and that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, I'm stopping you. Next question, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It actually probably comes to that issue anyway,

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But it was how Radovan Karadzic was able to influence policy over the Bosnian Serbs, whether Mr. Milosevic had more influence than he or whether Radovan Karadzic was the more influential over the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Absolutely my answer would be Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Milosevic was respected in certain circles in Bosnia, of course, but as I said, they considered that he was too weak and that he should have been more energetic in protecting the Serbs. And they criticised him for that. They reproached him for that. Mr. Karadzic was the be-all, end-all authority in Bosnia. And it was thanks to his positions but also he was a very well educated, broadly educated man, a scientist. He delved in literature and poetry so he enjoyed enormous respect in all circles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you able to put a date to that, when his influence over the Bosnian Serbs came about?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: You mean Mr. Karadzic. Well, I think that that was from the very beginning or, rather, first of all, in Bosnia, on a strictly national and religious basis, you had the formation of the SDA party, that is to say the Democratic Party of the Muslims under the Presidency of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. The second party to be formed was the Croatian party. The Serbs were not organised. And then the initiative came that a Serbian Democratic Party should be formed too. And it was the last party to be formed in that chain. And that raised Mr. Karadzic's rating because he was the initiator, and he was elected as the first president of that party. He was -- he conducted himself very wisely and skilfully. If you look at his speeches, they were the speeches of a very highly intellectual mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We know that Radovan Karadzic and President Milosevic were in fact not, in terms of politics, of the same parties, nor had they the same political beliefs.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was there a strong -- or how would you describe the political link between President Milosevic and Radovan Karadzic in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: When your house is burning, your house on is fire, all the inmates, everybody in the house tries to save what can be salvaged, even when they are in a confrontation themselves. And I think that's how the Serb people felt at that time. Their house was burning, but let's bridge the differences dividing us, the ideological ones, political ones. It's a to-be-or-not-to-be moment. A Shakespeare moment in fact. That's what it was for the Serbs then. That's where the link arose from and how they were linked. Unfortunately, this level of linkage was not maintained. After President Milosevic accepted the suggestions made by the West and established a border or, rather, sanctions vis-a-vis Republika Srpska, that's where the unbalance occurred and where Mrs. Milosevic's influence dropped and continued to decline and where Mr. Karadzic's influence was on the rise. It was the sanctions. The sanctions were a terrible blow to the Serb people, of course under pressure from the European Community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we've heard evidence that President Milosevic had to deal with the sanctions against his country. We know evidence and we've had evidence about that. As far as the dealings you had with President Milosevic, which, as you've told us, were on a daily -- daily basis, was there any question, from what you could see, as to whether he was operating a parallel policy, saying to you one thing but doing something else? Is there any question of that at all?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to say. After Carrington's paper fell through and Serbia rejected the document, President Milosevic later on tried to maintain those contacts. And I have to say that while we still had negotiations here and in Brussels, the European Community continuously insisted upon some sort of conspiratorial attitude. They would always say no records to be kept, no minutes to be kept, no notes to be kept, no statements to be given; what we are discussing is strictly confidential. Now, I was never quite clear on that, why that was, and I personally raised the question on many occasions but this was not respected and not much attention was paid to that, to the strictly confidential, because politicians would give statements for the press after the meetings. So after that, I myself began to withdraw. I drew further away from Mr. Milosevic because he continued to negotiate and -- but there were changes in Serbia that had taken place. Governments were changed. We had new elections every two years. We had six governments, I believe. We got through six governments in the space of nine years. So that was the situation. And we had a very turbulent political scene in Serbia during that period. And I was not a personage myself to be in a position to be told all these matters and confided in. I was, in a way, always an expert participant. That was the capacity I was in. So that later on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you for answering my questions, Professor Avramov. There will be some more questions. Before I sit down, Your Honours, there were two documents produced during the course of the examination-in-chief, the one marked DPH 990. If that could be made a Defence Exhibit. We now have a translation here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- so people are obviously listening to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: D243, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the other document, which is headed Order, Naredbu, DPH 984, if that could be given the next exhibit number of D244.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I also have a translation here of that, and I dare say it will be made available to the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think what we got is a translation of D244, which says "Order."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So we still have to get the translation of the first --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's been done as well. D243 has a translation as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the Court Deputy can check during the adjournment whether it should start from 242 rather than 243.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. We are going to break for 20 minutes. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the Chamber has considered the exercise of its discretion under paragraph 2 of its order, and we will allow you, if you wish, to ask additional questions. If you wish to ask additional questions, you should indicate the areas that you propose to cover. Do you wish to ask any additional questions; and if so, what are the areas?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, you are suggesting to me that within something that is supposed to be considered my Defence I put additional questions. In what is considered to be my Defence, that I put additional questions, that is just cynical and nothing else. Secondly, everything that Mr. Kay has put only dilutes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I am stopping you. I take it your answer is no. Professor. Professor. Professor, before you are asked questions by the Prosecutor, the Chamber would like to ask whether there is any other matter on which -- on which you would wish to express yourself briefly. Is there any other matter relevant to the -- to the issues that we are discussing on which you would wish to say anything? Briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, this case that you are examining is so complicated, and it consists of several different strata, so there would be a host of issues that could be raised. However, there is one thing that I wish to note. I think that you have reduced the entire case to a closed circle. The problem of Yugoslavia, or as it is called the territorial transformation thereof, is one that Newsweek devoted an entire issue to in 1990. An entire issue. I beg your pardon, just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, may I just remind you -- no. Let me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you permit me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What we are inviting you to do, what we would like you to do, since we believe it might be helpful, is for you to express your views on any matter that is relevant to the issues. We don't want to have a general discussion. If you can't identify any particular matter, then so be it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This is very concrete. This discusses the problem of the Balkans and how the Balkan issue will be resolved. This says that there will be a war in the Balkans. This speaks of alternatives in the way in which things will be rearranged and how the right to intervention, the right to interfere in the affairs of other states prohibited by the UN Charter is going to be changed altogether. So the entire question of the break-up of Yugoslavia has to be viewed in the broader context of previous preparations in terms of what would happen in Yugoslavia, and that came from outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to go back into history very much, but I think it's right, is it, that the late President Tito held the view that a weakened Serbia made for a stronger Yugoslavia? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Those are his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that that was one of the reasons why Vojvodina and Kosovo had the high level of autonomy that they did have.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In due course, a very famous memorandum was published which we'll deal with, probably not particularly with you, the SANU memorandum, at the end, or the middle, the end of the 1980s. Did that memorandum take the view that this approach of weakening Serbia was wrong?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: You see, I wouldn't want to go into that because I think that there are people who are far more competent in giving their opinions on the memorandum. I read it. I have it. After all, it's been translated into English so you can see it. As far as I understood the memorandum, the point of the memorandum was the unsatisfactory position, the unsatisfactory economic position of Serbia which, in a way, was used as a source of raw materials for other republics. And then there was another paradox. Absolutely. You're a legal man yourself, and you have the constitution that was translated into English. Our provinces actually had para-statal status. And not only that. Look at the following position: The two provinces had to give their approval when the constitution of Serbia was to be amended, but Serbia did not have the right to veto the amendment of the constitutions of the provinces. So that's a paradox, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you, I hope not rudely, but to try and bring you back to the question that I asked. And just generally, is it right that the thinking of the intellectuals who contributed to the SANU memorandum concluded that this weakening of Serbia by the autonomy of Kosovo and Vojvodina was a bad thing? Just yes or no and a few words of qualification at the most.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: My impression is, but also my profound conviction, I have to tell you that, is that is correct, you see, because you should not lose sight of the fact that people constantly keep forgetting, that the autonomy of Kosovo was abused. You see --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you so we can move forward. So, yes, that was the view of the intellectuals contributing to the memorandum. From you, because it's the first time you've dealt with this in this way, those who come from countries other than the former Yugoslavia, perhaps who come from countries with a long tradition of effective multi-party democratic government, may find it difficult to understand the significance of something like a memorandum coming from the Society of Arts and Sciences. This memorandum, even if we get others to deal with it in due course, was a seminal work for what was to follow, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: No, not quite. I wouldn't put it that way. Absolutely not. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond There is another matter, you see. The memorandum, in a way, was turned into a myth. Perhaps I can put it that way. Saying the memorandum of the Serb Academy meant the gravest condemnation of Serbia. I think that this was done intentionally. I repeat to you once again, I'm not competent for dealing with this matter. I believe that far more competent people than me will be dealing with the subject of the memorandum. But I would tell you that my impression is the following: In a situation when secessionist and terrorist movements developed in Croatia and in Slovenia, a balance had to be struck in order to accuse Serbia, too, and then some kind of Serb nationalism was invented. I assure you that it did not exist in Serbia. The memorandum is not a nationalist act at all. It is, if I can put it that way, a professional assessment of the economic status of Serbia, which is sliding towards being a Third World country and the situation as it was in the Third World at the time. So there was dissatisfaction in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Another thing too. Please. This memorandum was the draft of a draft. It was not a document that had been adopted by anyone. It was a preliminary draft that was drafted by three men only, members of the academy. Then the document was supposed to be taken to the committee --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: -- for the humanities and then further on to the Assembly and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I don't, we might get criticism of either you or me, and that would not be a good thing. I'll ask you to keep the answers short-ish. My point, and I think you've not necessarily rejected it, is that the opinions of something like the Society of Arts and Sciences was potentially - let's put it like that - was potentially very important in the former Yugoslavia where there was more limited opportunities for opposition and political groups to express their views. Would that just be roughly right? And then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: No. It cannot be put that way because a vast majority of the academy members had no idea of any memorandum because it had not gone through all these instances. It was only a preliminary draft. I personally can tell you that very good friends of mine, members of the academy, had no idea about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was actually asking you about the academy itself rather than the memorandum, and I asked it for this reason, you see: One of your answers where you were dealing with, I think, June of 1991, was to the effect that it wasn't just the accused who made decisions but that the conclusions that were reached were the conclusions of intellectuals, and you then said half of the SANU were involved in the decision. So I want to see how important this body is and then we'll move on from that. Can you help me? You -- yes.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: This is it precisely. May I? Sir, this is my summary of the things that we discussed but not the memorandum. There was not a single reference to the memorandum in our discussions, no. I have to tell you that, regrettably, two distinguished members of the academy, Mr. Ivic and Mr. Samardzic, especially Mr. Samardzic who was a very active historian, an exceptional scholar, you see. But this was the result, sir, not the memorandum.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So we're beginning to get an impression of how the SANU and its intellectuals may fit into the fabric of the former Yugoslavia when they contribute to this important document and you're able to make this document a central point of political discussion. You also said that it was not just the accused himself who made decisions. Can you just amplify that just a little bit for us? If he wasn't making decisions, who was? This is at the end of the period that you're telling us about; 1991. Who was making the decisions if not him?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Sir, in 1991 and even before that, a political game started outside the logic of the time that we lived in, outside all the rules of international law. In this political game, one of the protagonists was Mr. Milosevic, too. The central persons in this political game, which in my profound conviction was anti-legal, contradictory, because as Europe was uniting we had a fragmentation of Yugoslavia. We should have been talking about the need to democratise the company, not the need to establish ethnically pure states. So this was highly illogical. But allow me to say that the central issue was the following. Allow me to answer. Eleven countries of the European Union were against recognition. Only Germany was in favour of it, and the members of the EU yielded in Maastricht and let them have their way. Secondly --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Forgive me. Maybe I simply misunderstood your answer when you said that half of the SANU were involved and it wasn't just one person who made the decisions, because I thought you were referring to the fact that people other than the accused made decisions in and for Serbia. I wasn't talking about countries of the international community. Who -- who, other than the accused, made decisions for Serbia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Sir, I talked to you about the situation, the general situation, the discussion that took place and the quest for an answer to a crisis that the Serb people faced. I did not talk to you about passing decisions. Regrettably, from 1991 onwards all decisions depended on foreign factors, not on Serbia itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But in Serbia, madam, someone was making the decisions. That was this accused, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: No. Please. After all, at that time we had a multi-party system. We had a government. We had a parliament. So within that framework, there may have been things that came up this way or that way, but do not forget that we had nine elections during those ten years. It even annoyed all of us because there were so frequent changes of government. As I said, the situation was a very difficult one. I can assert absolutely that Mr. Milosevic always sought support in the Assembly, the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then made the final decisions himself.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I repeat to you yet again: He had certain powers as president to make certain decisions or to persuade people of the indispensability of certain decisions. But you have to bear in mind the fact that we were faced with ultimatums. We were under sanctions. We were isolated. Serbia was on the very brink of its existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll go back a little in time from 1991. Mr. Kay's questions premised on the basis that the crisis starts with the secession of Slovenia and Croatia. Is that your position or do you think the crisis started earlier than that?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: The crisis started earlier on, that's for sure, but in 1991, terrorist attacks were intensified, and then it started ascending.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If it started earlier, when did it start?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: You see, regrettably, as I've already said to you, what I'm saying to you is my own free assessment. I'm a professor who dealt in foreign policy -- foreign policy more than domestic policy, but you know what Klausewitz said, that foreign policy is only an extension of domestic policy. So I was interested, in a way, in these developments, and my impression is that Yugoslavia went from one crisis to another. With your permission, I would like to mention to you only a few central points. The year of 1945. During the war we had had a liberation war, but the revolutionary changes, the change of the system, nationalisation, expropriation and so on, all of that happened only later, only then in 1945. Then in 1948, the break-up with the Soviet Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I was only asking for dates and for your opinion about when it started and then we'll look at the event maybe --

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: But I'm telling you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You think it started in --

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Allow me to continue. No. Then there was this economic crisis. We kept having constant changes in the economic system, which led to major earthquakes. Kardelj, a Slovenian who was the ideologue who geared our post-war development. Every change that took place led to an earthquake within the country. Not only that, certain politicians were eliminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... next -- next?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Yes, and then Goli Otok, and then do you want me to tell you another thing? We were the only ones in Europe who had a concentration camp with 5.000 dead in it. Then the second stage in the 1960s. We moved on to a system of national economies, so there was further decentralisation. Yet again there were certain changes. Also, we had a system that was neither fish nor fowl. We had a market economy system which was completely different from the system that prevailed in the socialist countries, but then especially when this move to national economies was made in a situation when there is a process of economic integration in Europe, then this led to a disruption and to a severance of these ties. So that is how the crisis -- The next, the hardest of all, was the constitution of 1974. We at my faculty were opposed to that constitution. People were expelled from university, university teachers, and they were even taken to court and sentenced, but they believed that it was deeply geared against Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Since 1974.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I interrupt your account of dates just for this purpose: You were dismissed from the Communist Party in 1970, I think. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: No, 1951, 1952. That's when I was expelled. But then I was admitted yet again. And then in 1970 I left of my own free will.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I was expelled in January 1952, and then -- and then after a certain amount of time, this decision was annulled, and if you're interested in this specifically, I voted against decisions of the party organisation, and I was expelled immediately afterwards, and I was admitted into the party only a short time before that. And perhaps I can tell you that I was expelled the first time in 1946 after only a few months of being in the party. So I had this very tumultuous party life. And then again of my own free will I left the party in 1970. That's my party history. Let me tell you one more thing lest you have the wrong idea, sir: I did take part in the war. I belonged to the illegal movement --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've heard about your book Genocide Against The Serbs 1941 to 1945 and then 1991 --

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: [In English] No. Genocide in Yugoslavia in the Light of International Law. That was -- [Interpretation] I'm sorry. It was not only a genocide against the Serbs, nor did I describe only the genocide against the Serbs. This was a genocide against the Serbs, the Jews and the Roma. The Serb victims were the most numerous. Various theoreticians differ in their views. I relied on information from the Freiburg German archives. Croats are challenging the figures, saying that there weren't that many victims, but let's leave that aside. The largest number of victims were Serb, and then there were Jews --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us have the correct title of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I understood one of the books had been entitled Genocide Against the Serbs 1941 to 1945 and 1991 to 1992, but they -- the witness says otherwise. I'll check it overnight. But no doubt she's right. She may have got it with her.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I will give you a copy of the book, if I'm permitted to do that. When you asked me -- when Judge Robinson asked me, What does your book deal with, was that the question, your book on genocide, what period does it cover, I said it covered the period from 1941 to 1945 of the genocide against the Serbs, but I continued with my research on illegal movements. However, my book has been called [In English] Genocide of Yugoslavia in the Light of International law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well, but I-

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the translation of the title into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We know that it was an absolute imperative of the late Marsal Tito that there should be no embracing of nationalism in the Yugoslavia he led, and I'm just inquiring: Was your departure from the Communist Party in any way a reflection of your holding nationalist views?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: No. No. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I need to know.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Continuing on from the 1974 constitution, what do you say is the next event that really constitutes the beginning of the crisis into which this Court is inquiring?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: The death of Josip Broz caused a crisis of political authority because he was the undisputed dictator. By transferring power to a collective organ, a collective Supreme Commander comprising of representatives caused the crisis because conflicts between certain republics were so obvious that this collective body was not able to function, and that is where we had constant problems cropping up. The press wrote about that a lot, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... death of Tito in 1980 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 1980. The next event?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: In 1981, there was the rebellion of the Siptar minority in Kosovo, and this was a very strong and very militant rebellion with serious clashes in which many police officers were killed. This was in 1981. And then this continued until 1990. Negotiations were held at the time between the republics. It was not a very pleasant situation, and it finally ended with the crash, namely the secession.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I mean, I've given you a chance to list the causative events, and I notice you haven't dealt with the revocation of Kosovo's autonomy. Looking back, was that revocation instrumental in bringing the crisis on?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: You are deluded, sir, if you believe that autonomy was abolished in 1989 with the amendments to the Serbian constitution. Only some elements were abolished which had given Kosovo the status of a para-state. Autonomy remained. Actually, in a way, the status was restored which was in force before the constitution of 1974. However, the autonomy of Kosovo and Vojvodina remained untouched. The only things that were abolished were the elements which gave the provinces the status, as I said, the elements of statehood, the elements of statehood, which they -- which actually in Kosovo was abused, which was not the case in Vojvodina. In Kosovo, there was a mass populating that occurred, by Albanians, in Kosovo, and autonomy was abused to such an extent that the Albanians did not provide any elements to prove their nationality or citizenship. They were issued identity cards without any such proof.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You know that there is a debate about Kosovo, and let's put that on one side. What about Vojvodina? Do you think that the reduction or removal of Vojvodina's autonomy, of which we've had evidence, may have contributed to this unfolding of events? Because of course, along with Kosovo, Vojvodina was brought in and Serbia became more coherent and larger. Do you think that that's significant in this course of events? Why not?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Not greater. No, I don't believe that that was the case. It was used, you know. After the Carrington paper, everybody got wings. Everybody wanted to have some sort of independence. Everybody was in favour of further fragmentation. That is where the problem lies, not in the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're well before Carrington. I wanted you to help the Judges, if you'd be so good, with what part you thought the yogurt revolution, which on the material included Serbs from Kosovo being drafted in to create demonstrations in Novi Sad. What part do you think that may have played in these events?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: That the army demonstrated in Novi Sad, I have -- I don't know anything about that. That is first information that I have about that. I went there quite frequently. My husband comes from that part of the country, but this is the first time that I'm hearing that the army was there. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: There were demonstrations, demonstrations of citizens, yes, but not -- not demonstrations, but, if you allow, manifestations in favour of amendments or rallies in favour of amendments from 1990 -- 1989, because the Serbs wanted to have amendments which refer to their status. The question was why the autonomies on which Tito insisted in order to break up a balance and to reduce Serbia and in order to introduce some kind of balance amongst the republics because there were imbalances between certain republics. So the Serbs posed the question as follows: Why does a Krajina not have autonomy where there is a compact Serbian community? And also Slavonia. Why does that not have autonomy? Because that was never part of Croatia during the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Perhaps historians will explain this much better. But the Serbs put the question in this way: Why autonomy only in Serbia and not in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Vojvodina, just for a minute? You tell us you know the accused well from your dealings with him at the time, and you've explained what you believe to be the scope of the range of his influence and power to some degree. Do you accept that he would have had the ability to mobilise Serbs from Kosovo to go and demonstrate in Vojvodina? Do you accept that he would have had that ability?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: No. That's out of the question. Allow me, please. That is absolutely incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If -- let's just assume for the purposes of this argument, discussion, if that at time then it wasn't the accused who would be mobilising people to go and demonstrate in masses to achieve certain political objectives in Vojvodina, who would have been mobilising them for that purpose? Can you help us with a name?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Vojvodina has an absolute majority of Serbs. There was a census in Vojvodina recently. I don't want to mention any figures because I don't want to make a mistake, but 80 per cent of the population in Vojvodina are Serbs. You have a very small number of Slovaks, Romanians, Rusines, and there's also a Hungarian minority, about 300.000 out of two point something million. I don't have the figures here. If you're interested in the statistical figures, I could provide those for you. The citizens of Vojvodina protested. These were not demonstrations, sir. These were rallies, manifestations in support of amendments from 1989, not demonstrations. The demonstrations were held in Pristina against the amendments. That's the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move on with this last question. We know that in Kosovo there was all sorts of other issues arising from the KLA and terrorism. Just tell us, with all your knowledge and learning and experience, what was the real reason for reducing or eliminating Vojvodina's autonomy? Was there one?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: There was, because they had identical status, both provinces. So you cannot change the status of one and not change the status of the other. That is the problem. The point of the amendments was to deprive the provinces of the right of veto through which they were influencing the policy of Serbia. That was the only right we had. Serbia simply with these amendments became a unified state with two provinces, autonomous provinces which maintained and kept their parliament, their government, and other organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By the reduction or elimination of autonomy, Serbia became united again, became the size of state that Tito had feared. He was right to have fear for that size of Serbia, wasn't he, madam? Because at that size it went on, as we can see, to serve its interests at the expense of others.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Sir, that logic could be applied to Germany, to France, to Great Britain, and so on and so forth. Each country has its minorities. So why should -- for example, let's take the example of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. Why do that? It's logical that each country would like to maintain its unity. I am an expert on international law and I don't want to use that word, but a state has an active duty to preserve the system on its territory or the order on its territory. That is its international obligation. Therefore, each state must have the capacity to control and maintain a given order on its territory. Serbia did not have that, did not have that ability and that -- and it was something that it implemented through those amendments. Why were they so much against the autonomy of Krajina when the Serbian people enjoyed that right during the Austro-Hungarian Empire but not during the era of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I come to the next event in the extract of chronological events I'm asking you about, you said at one stage in your evidence that the accused used the phrase -- some phrase similar to "All Serbs living in the same state." What were the two occasions when you heard him use that phrase?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: First time he said that -- and this is according to the press. I wasn't present but I got that information from the press, I took that information from the press; at a meeting of the Central Committee. I cannot recall the exact date. I didn't think that that was so important so that I would look up the date again. When the party fell apart, the announced break-up of the party, it didn't fall apart completely, that will come later, but it broke apart into national Communist Parties which was in contradiction with what was stated under international principles. So then I don't know who it was of those present who mentioned or who said that Serbia cannot permit the break-up of a state -- of a state in which the Serbian people would be fragmented. After that, when these first terrorist attacks against Serbs occurred, these were group acts and there was a mass expulsion of Serbs, because at the end of 1991, we had over 200.000 Serb refugees arriving from Croatia. Then addressing the Serbs, he said, "We will use all possible means to protect you and to implement your wish that we all remain in one state," because this was also the request of Pale, of Bosnia, and the Republic of Srpska Krajina. Even before, you know, they outvoted the Republic of Serbia and Krajina, and Republika Srpska when they saw that Serbia would not declare a united integrated territory. This was an act of self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The phrase "Greater Serbia" has its own history and sometimes emotional consequences so let's not use that today, but it's clear that the idea of all Serbs living in one state is an idea that was around, that did exist and can even find expression in the accused in the way you've described; correct?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I don't know. I was following that, but I cannot say that I followed the entire process. I followed some of it and some of it not, so I cannot recall in which context Mr. Milosevic used that. I'm using it in terms of what I know, what I experienced and the things that I participated in. Yes, you are absolutely right. He -- he does have -- or it has an emotional connotation, but it can also be a pejorative idea promoted by the Austro-Hungarian Empire in 1914. Any time that Serbia was to have been described as aggressive in a way, this phrase was resorted to. Serbia had two opportunities, really, to achieve greatness; in 1916 when the allies asked it to give up the idea of Yugoslavia and to receive borders including Palanka, the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina and a part of Slavonia. Serbia rejected that in favour of the unification of the Southern Slavs in order to encompass and fulfil the requests of a part of the Croatian and Dalmatian intelligence Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond so that they would overthrow the Austro-Hungarian burden or rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll go back to the chronology in a minute, but before I do, something that may help us all is this: You've used -- made reference to Ireland and Great Britain. Lots of Irish live in England. Come to that, they live in America. And in every country there are residents in the country -- or nearly every country there are residents from neighbouring states, and it may be that there are some 5.000 identifiable groups in the world living in 200 states. I don't know. What we need to know - and I don't mean this offensively, Professor Avramov - is what's so special about the Serbs that they are entitled to pursue, at the interests of others, the notion that they can all live in one state? Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Serbs never neglected the interests of other states, but this is a natural right of every people. Just look at what a greater Germany did. Why would the unification of Germany -- it would be the correction of a historical mistake, because Germany was defeated in two world wars. And why would it be such a terrible sin from Serbia, which fought for this new Europe in two world wars, sacrifice one-third of its population for a European order which it fought for. Why would this be such a large sin? Well, perhaps we could say well, all right, let them live. Please. Even the Chinese would like to have Taiwan as part of their country. So there are many other such examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The question is: What's so special about Serbia or Serbs? You give the example of Germany, and I must ask you this question: Did the unification of Germany involve massive ethnic movements and ethnic cleansing of minorities who happened not to be Germans found in one part of the united Germany or the other? Did it?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Well, actually there was, but it wasn't really talked about very much. But at the same time, I will tell you that there were no movements of population from Serbia. If I can give you an example. In Hungary in 1918, 250.000 Serbs lived, and today there are only 5.000 of them there. They have been partly assimilated, partly they have been relocated, and so on and so forth. Serbia is the only country in Europe, I would say, in which the minorities were allowed to flourish, and they did not lessen in numbers but their numbers increased. That is one thing. Now, why did the Serbs wish one state? The continuity of the suffering of the Serbian people going back for a hundred years is one of the elements because of which the Serbs believed that they did have a legal right and that this was the only way to protect themselves. Sir, the Serbs have suffered terribly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is there any other reason, apart from Serbs as historical victims, that justified their pursuit of the notion that they should all live in one state at whatever cost to others?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I don't see any reason. If in 1915 the forces of -- of the Entente accepted the unification of the Serbian people as their objective, they accepted this, the forces of Entente, and that was their guiding idea and the guiding idea of the Serbian people in the heroic fight that they endured. So I do not see the danger. I do not see any people. Who are the people who suffered under the Serbian boot? I can't think of any. I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course, determining the issues of what happened and whether they were crimes and so on and who is responsible is entirely a matter for the Judges. You've expressed some views, and I want to ask you one thing about them, and it's this: In your view, is protection of the Serbs from suffering a matter of such priority as it would justify killing and moving people from territories that Serbs wished to assume and control as their own? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I don't know. Please. During the existence of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, very many Croats remained to live in Knin even though Knin was always a majority Serb town. A lot of Croats remained, though, and nothing -- they came to no harm. Nothing happened to them. So I don't see what is the fault of the Serbs. The other side -- please. Once a war starts, I am of deeply anti-war conviction, and I have participated in the work of many peace organisations, but once this tragedy, the most serious tragedy does occur and when our crisis grew into this tragic war, then you know war has its own logic; kill or be killed. That is one thing. The psychology of people changes. You as a lawyer, and myself also as a legal person, read a lot. Especially read a lot when I was writing the book on genocide. This collective spirit which takes over the threatened nation, then when you look at the killing of your -- when you see how your own family is killed, the only thing that remains is bitter revenge, and this is something that happened. You understand, terrible crimes, sir. I never claimed that there were no crimes. Quite the reverse, sir; there were crimes committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the presentation of exhibits in the course of the Defence case is something we are working on as to the best and most economic procedure, but for the time being today, can we hand them in individually?
