utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is an article, Professor, of yours. If it can be distributed. It's called Models of Serbhood and you must obviously have a second or so, or a minute or so to remind yourself that it's written by you and when. You will see, I think, that this is dated the 23rd of August, 1996, in Belgrade. Do you remember writing this article?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I never wrote an article under such a title, never. I would have to read it to see. As far as I can see, the first sentences are not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will come back to this article, if necessary, tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I would like to know where this was published.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Absolutely. We'll deal with that tomorrow. But --

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: As I say --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you be good enough, for the time being, to save time, we're coming towards what the court may decide is the end of the day but if not for us... If you come down one, two, three, four, five paragraphs, to the end the paragraph on the first page, and you'll --

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Not an article under that title, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But we then come to this paragraph which reflects partly your views on this court and partly your views under -- about two other individuals, and it says the following and I'll read it: "I have been following the work of this institution since the beginning. I shun the use of the term 'court' since the judiciary is a high-minded institution to every lawyer. I have been shocked by the fact that since its inception to this date its activity has been of a markedly anti-Serb orientation."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, giving some thought to this, I mean the witness has said it's not her article.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: She has not said it's not her article.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to say something now at this point? I never wrote an article under that heading, under that title. This particular paragraph seems to me to be a paragraph taken from one of my articles, yes, that is true, and that is what I said. So let me tell you at the outset: I was present -- if you will allow me to finish. May I please be allowed to continue and explain to you. Yes, I was highly critical and am highly critical towards this Tribunal; however, I considered that it was my duty to come here to testify so that we can arrive at the truth. I have expressed my views and, sir, I attended the preliminary conference for the establishment of this particular Tribunal, which was organised by the United Nations, and that meeting was held in Vancouver on the basis of expert opinion and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: -- there were 87 experts present --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: -- I was among them and I took the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, please answer the questions asked by counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've taken you to this paragraph not particularly to turn to the issue of your attitude to the Tribunal but simply to establish that this is indeed your work. I'm more interested in the following paragraph, which reads as follows -- or the following sentence, I beg your pardon: "The primary and the most serious crime, the one committed by the Croats and Muslims resulting in bloodshed, has been disregarded. I was shocked also as a member of the Serbian people, especially when an indictment was issued against President Karadzic and General Mladic, the two greatest figures in recent Serbian history." You've told us your very favourable views of Radovan Karadzic. This article, written a year and a month after Srebrenica, expresses your views of General Mladic. Do you still hold those views?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: As for General Mladic, a man I met several times, I have a very high opinion of him as a soldier. I know some heroic feats of his in which he saved civilians, both Muslim and Serb civilians. I also know of him from the times when he was - and that was the turning point in his life - when he was in Republika Srpska Krajina as the commander. He was later moved to Republika Srpska. But I also know that at the military academy, he slept in the bed next to a Croat, a cadet attending the military academy, and learning about this colleague of his, and they were very close during their studies at the academy, he moved to -- into the Croatian army subsequently and committed serious crimes in Ogulin. I know about that. I also know that that was a turning point in his life with respect to his attitude towards brotherhood and unity, as it was. And I also know that this made his mind up. He decided to move to the Serb army and to place himself at the head of the Serb army. That's what I know about General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I asked you these questions because I want to come back to the question I asked you at the beginning of this short passage. Is it your view that the crimes committed or that the killings committed in the Serb interest were in fact all justified for the reason that you've identified, that is, the fear of Serbs of being yet again victims?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: The fear that the Serbs felt was enormous, to the effect that the 1941 genocide would be repeated, and that fear quite certainly caused or led to a series of crimes or retaliation or acts of revenge. I condemn all crime. There is no justification for a single crime committed in anybody's name, on anybody's behalf. But I would like to repeat that crimes, too, and I have studied them on a parallel basis from the conflicts in Asia, in America, various wars throughout the world to the present day, that every war, each and every war and each and every crime must be placed in a given historical context, and only once you have done that can you understand what actually took place, and only then on the basis of that can you give your own judgement about it. I would like to repeat that as to your Tribunal, I held a report, I delivered a report at the preliminary meeting. None of the experts wanted the Tribunal, that court, to be set up. I was against its inception, and I wrote in that light.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was saying that we don't need all of that evidence. And we can work until 2.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then let me move on from those questions and answers to the next event that I wanted to ask you about and I will ask you about, and it's this: You will remember how following the miners' strike in Kosovo there were enormous demonstrations on the streets of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I can't quite -- or, rather, I'm not quite sure that I was in Belgrade at the time. Perhaps I was. I can't remember for sure. I can't remember those exact demonstrations, but, yes, there were demonstrations in Belgrade. As to the exact date and the exact demonstrations you referred to, I don't know which they are. There were many demonstrations. There were casualties, dead people in the demonstrations, especially the 9th of March demonstrations. Yes, there were. But as I say, I don't know the specific demonstrations you're referring to. Let me say straight away that I myself was not somebody who took part in demonstrations ever so I can't really speak about that. I didn't take part in any demonstrations because of my age. I did take part in demonstrations as a student prior to the Second World War when I was that age.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the time of these demonstrations, the then-President Dizdarevic was unable to calm the crowd despite his calls for brotherhood and unity, and eventually the accused had his way and emergency powers were issued, and this was the first time that he was able to have control or to have the army, the JNA, working in his interest on the territory of Serbia. You remember that, do you?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I did not take part in that so I really can't say whether Mr. Milosevic ordered that or anything else. I can't testify about something I don't know about first hand, where I was not present. Perhaps he did, perhaps he didn't. I don't know. He'll be best able to tell you, because I am not informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two things, madam, just two things, because we have to look at quite particularly how these events have a sequence to them. Do you think that the accused at the time of the miner's strike and the grant of special powers to bring the army to Kosovo, do you think that at that time the accused had the ability to get the people onto the street to work for him and to support his objectives? Do you?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic had no reason to do that, bring the people out, because there was such a great deal of revolt in Serbia that he didn't need to do that. That's the first point. And secondly, the main demonstrations were launched by the opposition parties, as far as I remember, not the ruling party. And as far as I remember, but let me repeat, that I travelled quite a bit and spent quite a lot of time abroad so that I cannot recall, and as I say I don't think I was in Belgrade at the time, so I can't remember that, but as I say, your question is a very generalised one or, rather, the observation you make is rather generalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second question about the same demonstration, and subject to translation that I'll deal with overnight, but if part of the accused's address to that mass gathering was to the effect, "No price and no force on earth can stop the Serbian people," did that accord with your understanding of how he thought at that time?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I can't say. I can't confirm or assert. I didn't hear it. I didn't hear him say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To say such a thing, and we'll look at it, I hope, tomorrow -- of course, I'll withdraw the question completely if we don't, but to say such a thing is a call to nationalism, madam, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I don't know what context that was stated in. I don't know when it was stated. And as far as the demonstrations or, rather, the miner's strike is concerned, do you mean the strike in Kolubara, Kolubara mine, or do you mean the strike in Kosovo? Which strike did you mean? Which miner's strike were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Ah, in Kosovo. The strike in Kosovo. That was staged. It was a theatre production which was to demonstrate the grave situation that the miners live in. And this was all for the benefit of the European Union or whatever, the European Community or whoever it was who came, I can't remember. But I know for a fact that it was all staged in order to demonstrate the suffering of the Albanians. Certainly there were Albanian casualties, Albanian victims, but you know there were atrocious crimes committed. Let me remind you the atrocity of Martinovic when he was impaled upon a bottle. Danilo Malilovic was killed in front of his mother's eyes. So there were atrocious crimes, and I condemn all crimes, whether they be Serb crimes or Albanian crimes or anybody else's crimes. There were crimes, yes, sir, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll start another topic. I may not be able to finish it this morning. I'll do my best. There was a magazine called Epoka, published for a couple of years in about 1991 and revived later. Was effectively the magazine of the accused's SPS party; correct?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: I wasn't kept abreast of all the magazines for the simple reason that I wasn't technically able to read them all. I never belonged to the SPS myself, so I wasn't kept abreast of their activities. I was able to follow many other magazines and I subscribed to many magazines, professional and otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is what I have said about Epoka correct, it was the SPS magazine? Yes or no. We will have the original here tomorrow, you see. I haven't got --

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: Probably he was -- it was, but I really don't know. I can't say. I simply don't know. Let me repeat. I didn't buy the Epoka magazine, for instance. I didn't read it. I wasn't a subscriber, just as I didn't read Vreme. There are a hundred or so periodicals that are published in Belgrade, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, about the Belgrade initiative. You know about that. What did that plan?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: It was a plan which I showed you the variants of. That was the Belgrade initiative, the two or three points as variations. It was a meeting with the representatives of the Krajina, of Republika Srpska or, rather, they hadn't been proclaimed as such yet, so find a peaceful settlement to the Serb question in Croatia and Bosnia, because the Serb question was put on the agenda automatically, spontaneously, when ethnically pure states were being set up with the acquiescence of the European Community.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Variant 1 and Variant 2 document, the exhibit number for which I'm afraid I've forgotten, just one thing because I didn't understand it as you read it over to me and I've only just looked at a translation, did that inevitably involve large transfers of population?

utterances.speaker: SMILJA AVRAMOV
utterances.text: No, not at all. Without any transference of the population. It just referred to the ways and means of solving problems where the majority population was Serb, and that is why the proposal was put forward in that way. And we hitched onto that idea of creating a sort of condominium, in fact, so that we would have equidistance both with respect to the Serbs vis-a-vis Croatia and vis-a-vis Serbia, that that was the most suitable variant in view of all the mixed marriages. And don't forget, with all the decentralisation and all the economies, all the economies were linked in one way or another, and the quakes that happened happened in the economy, the reverberations were felt throughout Yugoslavia, and that is what we were geared towards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next exercise involves some exhibits. Might it be easier - I see I've probably got two minutes - to wait until I have the original magazine tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Nice. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond In that case, we'll adjourn for today. Before we adjourn, Mr. Milosevic, I take this opportunity to remind you that the Chamber's order envisages the Court-assigned counsel approaching you for instructions. I encourage you to take advantage of that opportunity and to communicate with him. Professor, we are going to adjourn for the evening. Mr. Milosevic, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I have already said that this is a question of principle and that I do not accept you to rescind my right to my own Defence or to diminish that right in any way. I have nothing to do with your counsel. He does not represent me. He represents you. What he is doing here is not my Defence. Mr. Kay could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. We have heard that. Professor, we're going to take the adjournment for the afternoon. You will return tomorrow morning at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether you're aware of the fact that I'm due to leave tomorrow. I don't know the exact time. Sometime in the afternoon, anyway. I have a flight, whether it's 2.00 or 3.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe we'll be finished with you in time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, according to my flight, which is, I think, at 2.00 or 3.00 in the afternoon, I think that I would have to leave The Hague at about 1.00 to give me enough time to reach the airport and catch my flight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I would be available if we begin at 9.30. Is that when we begin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, we begin at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. 9.00. Then I would be available until 11.30, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 8th day of September, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.00 p.m.,
